# The problem: Duel: play an invented territory game against a pool of scripted opponents

Play an invented two-player board game, "spore", against a fixed pool of scripted opponents. The policy is one player; it chooses its move each turn.

**The board.** A connected graph of about 30 cells. Each cell is worth 1, 2 or 5 points (about 60% are worth 1, 25% worth 2, 15% worth 5). Each player starts owning one *home* cell (worth 1); the two homes are far apart. All other cells start empty.

**A turn.** Players alternate. On your turn you must *claim* one empty cell that is adjacent to at least one cell you own; it becomes yours. Then *flips*: every opponent cell adjacent to the cell you just claimed (except the opponent's home, which never flips) becomes yours if, counting after your claim, you own at least as many of its neighbours as its owner does. Flips are decided all at once from the board right after the claim and do not chain: a flipped cell does not trigger further flips. A player with no legal claim (no empty cell next to its cells) passes and the other player continues.

**The end.** The game ends when no empty cell is left (about 30 claims in all, roughly half of them yours). Each player scores the points of the cells it owns at the end.

**One decision** = choosing which cell to claim. The **candidates** are your legal claims, in a random order (cells are also numbered at random). When there is only one legal claim it is taken automatically.

**Instances and cost.** An instance is 24 games on freshly generated boards of one family: 6 against each of the 4 opponents in the pool, moving first in half of them. The opponents are scripted players with different, fixed behaviour; their logic and identity are hidden, and you never see their future moves. The instance's **cost** is 100 x the opponents' share of all points scored in its games (in [0, 100]; the board's points are always all claimed). The **gap** is 100 x cost / the cost of Code Zero (the policy that always takes the first candidate, i.e. a random legal claim) on the same instance: Code Zero scores 100, lower is better. An opponent always keeps at least its home, so 0 is impossible; there is no known best.

Three training families, differing in board shape: `grid` (a 6 x 6 square grid, 4 random cells removed, 4 neighbours per cell), `hex` (a 6 x 5 hexagonal grid, 2 cells removed, up to 6 neighbours) and `web` (32 random points, each joined to its 3 nearest). # The problem: Duel: play an invented territory game against a pool of scripted opponents

Play an invented two-player board game, "spore", against a fixed pool of scripted opponents. The policy is one player; it chooses its move each turn.

**The board.** A connected graph of about 30 cells. Each cell is worth 1, 2 or 5 points (about 60% are worth 1, 25% worth 2, 15% worth 5). Each player starts owning one *home* cell (worth 1); the two homes are far apart. All other cells start empty.

**A turn.** Players alternate. On your turn you must *claim* one empty cell that is adjacent to at least one cell you own; it becomes yours. Then *flips*: every opponent cell adjacent to the cell you just claimed (except the opponent's home, which never flips) becomes yours if, counting after your claim, you own at least as many of its neighbours as its owner does. Flips are decided all at once from the board right after the claim and do not chain: a flipped cell does not trigger further flips. A player with no legal claim (no empty cell next to its cells) passes and the other player continues.

**The end.** The game ends when no empty cell is left (about 30 claims in all, roughly half of them yours). Each player scores the points of the cells it owns at the end.

**One decision** = choosing which cell to claim. The **candidates** are your legal claims, in a random order (cells are also numbered at random). When there is only one legal claim it is taken automatically.

**Instances and cost.** An instance is 24 games on freshly generated boards of one family: 6 against each of the 4 opponents in the pool, moving first in half of them. The opponents are scripted players with different, fixed behaviour; their logic and identity are hidden, and you never see their future moves. The instance's **cost** is 100 x the opponents' share of all points scored in its games (in [0, 100]; the board's points are always all claimed). The **gap** is 100 x cost / the cost of Code Zero (the policy that always takes the first candidate, i.e. a random legal claim) on the same instance: Code Zero scores 100, lower is better. An opponent always keeps at least its home, so 0 is impossible; there is no known best.

# The problem: Duel: play an invented territory game against a pool of scripted opponents

Play an invented two-player board game, "spore", against a fixed pool of scripted opponents. The policy is one player; it chooses its move each turn.

**The board.** A connected graph of about 30 cells. Each cell is worth 1, 2 or 5 points (about 60% are worth 1, 25% worth 2, 15% worth 5). Each player starts owning one *home* cell (worth 1); the two homes are far apart. All other cells start empty.

**A turn.** Players alternate. On your turn you must *claim* one empty cell that is adjacent to at least one cell you own; it becomes yours. Then *flips*: every opponent cell adjacent to the cell you just claimed (except the opponent's home, which never flips) becomes yours if, counting after your claim, you own at least as many of its neighbours as its owner does. Flips are decided all at once from the board right after the claim and do not chain: a flipped cell does not trigger further flips. A player with no legal claim (no empty cell next to its cells) passes and the other player continues.

**The end.** The game ends when no empty cell is left (about 30 claims in all, roughly half of them yours). Each player scores the points of the cells it owns at the end.

**One decision** = choosing which cell to claim. The **candidates** are your legal claims, in a random order (cells are also numbered at random). When there is only one legal claim it is taken automatically.

**Instances and cost.** An instance is 24 games on freshly generated boards of one family: 6 against each of the 4 opponents in the pool, moving first in half of them. The opponents are scripted players with different, fixed behaviour; their logic and identity are hidden, and you never see their future moves. The instance's **cost** is 100 x the opponents' share of all points scored in its games (in [0, 100]; the board's points are always all claimed). The **gap** is 100 x cost / the cost of Code Zero (the policy that always takes the first candidate, i.e. a random legal claim) on the same instance: Code Zero scores 100, lower is better. An opponent always keeps at least its home, so 0 is impossible; there is no known best.

Three training families, differing in board shape: `grid` (a 6 x 6 square grid, 4 random cells removed, 4 neighbours per cell), `hex` (a 6 x 5 hexagonal grid, 2 cells removed, up to 6 neighbours) and `web` (32 random points, each joined to its 3 nearest). The test split adds a board shape that training never shows.

Play an invented two-player board game, "spore", against a fixed pool of scripted opponents. The policy is one player; it chooses its move each turn.

# The problem: Duel: play an invented territory game against a pool of scripted opponents

Play an invented two-player board game, "spore", against a fixed pool of scripted opponents. The policy is one player; it chooses its move each turn.

**The board.** A connected graph of about 30 cells. Each cell is worth 1, 2 or 5 points (about 60% are worth 1, 25% worth 2, 15% worth 5). Each player starts owning one *home* cell (worth 1); the two homes are far apart. All other cells start empty.

**A turn.** Players alternate. On your turn you must *claim* one empty cell that is adjacent to at least one cell you own; it becomes yours. Then *flips*: every opponent cell adjacent to the cell you just claimed (except the opponent's home, which never flips) becomes yours if, counting after your claim, you own at least as many of its neighbours as its owner does. Flips are decided all at once from the board right after the claim and do not chain: a flipped cell does not trigger further flips. A player with no legal claim (no empty cell next to its cells) passes and the other player continues.

**The end.** The game ends when no empty cell is left (about 30 claims in all, roughly half of them yours). Each player scores the points of the cells it owns at the end.

**One decision** = choosing which cell to claim. The **candidates** are your legal claims, in a random order (cells are also numbered at random). When there is only one legal claim it is taken automatically.

**Instances and cost.** An instance is 24 games on freshly generated boards of one family: 6 against each of the 4 opponents in the pool, moving first in half of them. The opponents are scripted players with different, fixed behaviour; their logic and identity are hidden, and you never see their future moves. The instance's **cost** is 100 x the opponents' share of all points scored in its games (in [0, 100]; the board's points are always all claimed). The **gap** is 100 x cost / the cost of Code Zero (the policy that always takes the first candidate, i.e. a random legal claim) on the same instance: Code Zero scores 100, lower is better. An opponent always keeps at least its home, so 0 is impossible; there is no known best.

Three training families, differing in board shape: `grid` (a 6 x 6 square grid, 4 random cells removed, 4 neighbours per cell), `hex` (a 6 x 5 hexagonal grid, 2 cells removed, up to 6 neighbours) and `web` (32 random points, each joined to its 3 nearest). The test split adds a board shape that training never shows.

```python
import numpy as np
from collections import deque

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Sum of points in the opponent-free connected pocket reachable from each candidate (0 if candidate not opponent-free), divided by 30."""
    N = owner.shape[0]
    E = (owner == 0)
    opp = (owner == -1)
    oppn = adjacency.astype(int) @ opp.astype(int)
    free = E & (oppn == 0)

    values = np.zeros(moves.shape[0], dtype=float)
    for i, c in enumerate(moves):
        if not free[c]:
            continue
        # BFS over adjacency restricted to `free`, starting at c
        visited = np.zeros(N, dtype=bool)
        visited[c] = True
        queue = deque([c])
        total = 0
        while queue:
            u = queue.popleft()
            total += points[u]
            nbrs = np.where(adjacency[u] & free & ~visited)[0]
            for v in nbrs:
                visited[v] = True
                queue.append(v)
        values[i] = total / 30.0
    return values
```

Play an invented two-player board game, "spore", against a fixed pool of scripted opponents. The policy is one player; it chooses its move each turn.

**The board.** A connected graph of about 30 cells. Each cell is worth 1, 2 or 5 points (about 60% are worth 1, 25% worth 2, 15% worth 5). Each player starts owning one *home* cell (worth 1); the two homes are far apart. All other cells start empty.

**A turn.** Players alternate. On your turn you must *claim* one empty cell that is adjacent to at least one cell you own; it becomes yours. Then *flips*: every opponent cell adjacent to the cell you just claimed (except the opponent's home, which never flips) becomes yours if, counting after your claim, you own at least as many of its neighbours as its owner does. Flips are decided all at once from the board right after the claim and do not chain: a flipped cell does not trigger further flips. A player with no legal claim (no empty cell next to its cells) passes and the other player continues.

**The end.** The game ends when no empty cell is left (about 30 claims in all, roughly half of them yours). Each player scores the points of the cells it owns at the end.

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Net swing in points from this claim's flips minus the value the opponent can flip straight back next turn from the emptied neighbourhood."""
    N = owner.shape[0]
    mine = (owner == 1)
    opp = (owner == -1)
    empty = (owner == 0)
    pts = points.astype(np.float64)
    idx = np.arange(N)

    A1 = adjacency @ mine.astype(np.int64)
    Ao = adjacency @ opp.astype(np.int64)

    adj_c = adjacency[moves]                                   # (k, N)
    not_opp_home = idx != homes[1]
    flippable = adj_c & opp[None, :] & not_opp_home[None, :] & (A1[None, :] + 1 >= Ao[None, :])

    # points gained by flipping
    gain = (flippable * pts[None, :]).sum(axis=1)

    # after my claim + flips: my count and opp count per opponent cell that remains
    flips_per_cell = flippable.sum(axis=0)                     # (N,) how many candidates flip cell j
    # per-candidate remaining opp cells with updated neighbour counts
    opp_rem = opp[None, :] & ~flippable                        # (k, N)
    A1b = A1[None, :] + flippable.astype(np.int64)             # my neighbours after flips (approx: +1 from claim only on c)
    # account for my new cell c contributing to its own neighbours
    A1b = A1b + adj_c.astype(np.int64)
    Aob = (opp_rem.astype(np.int64) @ adjacency.astype(np.int64))  # (k, N)

    # opponent's best recapture: for each candidate, look at empty cells e adjacent to remaining opp cells,
    # that opp could claim and then flip my cells j (not my home) with Aob[j]+1 >= A1b[j]
    my_rem = mine[None, :] | flippable                         # my cells (including newly flipped) per candidate
    not_my_home = idx != homes[0]
    # can-be-flipped-back mask depends on candidate via A1b/Aob
    back_flippable = my_rem & not_my_home[None, :] & ((Aob + 1) >= A1b)  # (k, N)

    # empty cells adjacent to remaining opp territory (opp can claim there)
    opp_frontier = empty[None, :] & (adj_c & opp_rem).any(axis=0)[None, :] & (opp_rem @ adjacency.astype(np.int64) > 0)
    # (k, N) : empty cell e that opp can claim now (adjacent to opp_rem)
    opp_legal = empty[None, :] & (opp_rem.astype(np.int64) @ adjacency.astype(np.int64) > 0)

    # loss from recapture: for each legal opp cell e, points[e] claimed + points of my cells it flips back
    back_pts = (back_flippable * pts[None, :])                          # (k, N) points at risk per my cell
    recapture_value = pts[None, :] + (adjacency.astype(np.float64) @ back_pts.T).T  # (k, N) value if e claimed
    big_neg = np.where(opp_legal, recapture_value, -1.0)
    worst = big_neg.max(axis=1)
    worst = np.maximum(worst, 0.0)

    return (gain - worst) / 15.0
feature.measures: Net swing in points from this claim's flips minus the value the opponent can flip straight back next turn from the emptied neighbourhood.

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Sum over empty cells at graph distance 2 from the candidate of points / (1 + opponent pressure), i.e. two-step reach discounted by how contested it is, divided by 30."""
    N = owner.shape[0]
    E = (owner == 0)
    opp = (owner == -1)
    A = adjacency.astype(np.float64)
    Ao = A @ opp.astype(np.float64)  # opponent neighbours per cell
    pts = points.astype(np.float64)
    # two-step reach: empty cells two hops from candidate (vectorised)
    A_moves = adjacency[moves].astype(np.float64)  # (k, N)
    reach1 = A_moves * E[None, :]
    reach2 = (reach1 @ A) * E[None, :]
    reach2 = reach2 * (1.0 - A_moves)  # exclude distance-1 cells
    # discount each two-step cell by opponent pressure (1/(1+count))
    discount = (1.0 / (1.0 + Ao))[None, :]
    values = (reach2 * discount * pts[None, :]).sum(axis=1) / 30.0
    return values

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Net flip balance spread over the opponent's best reply: points I would flip now minus the points the opponent's single best flip-back could take, scaled by how much of the game is left, /15."""
    N = owner.shape[0]
    mine = (owner == 1)
    opp = (owner == -1)
    empty = (owner == 0)
    A1 = adjacency @ mine.astype(np.int64)
    Ao = adjacency @ opp.astype(np.int64)
    pts = points.astype(np.float64)
    my_home = homes[0]
    opp_home = homes[1]
    not_my_home = np.ones(N, dtype=bool); not_my_home[my_home] = False
    not_opp_home = np.ones(N, dtype=bool); not_opp_home[opp_home] = False

    adj_moves = adjacency[moves]
    is_opp = opp[None, :] & not_opp_home[None, :]
    flip = adj_moves & is_opp & (A1[None, :] + 1 >= Ao[None, :])
    gain = (flip * pts[None, :]).sum(1)

    A1b = A1[None, :] + adj_moves.astype(np.int64) + flip.astype(np.int64) @ adjacency.astype(np.int64)
    Aob = Ao[None, :] - flip.astype(np.int64) @ adjacency.astype(np.int64)

    legal_e = empty[None, :] & (Aob > 0) & ~adj_moves
    adj_j = adjacency[None, :, :]
    mymask = (mine & not_my_home)[None, None, :]
    cond_j = (Aob[:, None, :] + 1 >= A1b[:, None, :])
    fb = legal_e[:, :, None] & adj_j & mymask & cond_j
    loss_per_e = (fb * pts[None, None, :]).sum(2)
    loss = loss_per_e.max(1)

    # spread: how many distinct empty cells offer a profitable flip-back (0..3), as a "breadth" measure
    profitable = (loss_per_e > 0).sum(1).astype(np.float64)
    breadth = np.minimum(profitable, 3.0) / 3.0

    # remaining-game weighting: early claims are less costly to expose than late ones
    remaining = max(N - 2 - turn, 0)
    frac = remaining / float(max(N - 2, 1))

    net = (gain - loss) / 15.0
    # amplify net when many flip-back options exist (opponent has choices), damp when game nearly over
    return net * (0.5 + 0.5 * breadth) * (0.3 + 0.7 * frac)
feature.measures: Net flip balance spread over the opponent's best reply: points I would flip now minus the points the opponent's single best flip-back could take, scaled by how much of the game is left, /15.

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Negative (normalised) best one-ply grab value available to the opponent after my claim and its flips."""
    N = owner.shape[0]
    my_home = homes[0]
    opp_home = homes[1]
    mine = (owner == 1)
    opp = (owner == -1)
    empty = (owner == 0)
    A1 = adjacency @ mine.astype(np.int64)
    Ao = adjacency @ opp.astype(np.int64)
    pts = points.astype(np.float64)

    out = np.zeros(moves.shape[0], dtype=np.float64)
    for idx in range(moves.shape[0]):
        c = moves[idx]
        # flips: opponent cells adjacent to c, not opp home, with A1[j]+1 >= Ao[j]
        adj_c = adjacency[c]
        flips = adj_c & opp & (np.arange(N) != opp_home) & ((A1 + 1) >= Ao)
        mine2 = mine.copy()
        mine2[c] = True
        mine2 |= flips
        opp2 = opp & ~flips
        A1b = adjacency @ mine2.astype(np.int64)
        Aob = adjacency @ opp2.astype(np.int64)
        legal_e = empty & (Aob > 0)
        if not legal_e.any():
            out[idx] = 0.0
            continue
        # gain[e] = points[e] + sum over j adjacent to e with mine2[j], j != my home, Aob[j]+1 >= A1b[j]
        flip_back_mask = mine2 & (np.arange(N) != my_home) & ((Aob + 1) >= A1b)
        flip_back_pts = np.where(flip_back_mask, pts, 0.0)
        # for each empty e: sum of flip_back_pts over neighbours
        gain = pts + adjacency @ flip_back_pts
        best = gain[legal_e].max()
        out[idx] = -best / 30.0
    return out

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Negative points of each candidate times the capped count of empty neighbours from which the opponent could claim and flip it next turn."""
    N = owner.shape[0]
    my = (owner == 1)
    opp = (owner == -1)
    empty = (owner == 0)
    opp_home = homes[1]

    A1 = adjacency @ my.astype(np.int64)      # my neighbours per cell
    Ao = adjacency @ opp.astype(np.int64)    # opponent neighbours per cell

    # opponent cells that would flip if I claim c (per candidate)
    # flips[j] = opp cell j adjacent to c, j != opp home, A1[j] + 1 >= Ao[j]
    adj_c = adjacency[moves]                 # (k, N)
    is_opp = opp[None, :]
    not_home = np.ones(N, dtype=bool)
    not_home[opp_home] = False
    flip_cond = (A1[None, :] + 1 >= Ao[None, :])
    flips = adj_c & is_opp & not_home[None, :] & flip_cond   # (k, N)

    f_nb = flips.astype(np.int64)            # (k, N) flipped neighbours of c

    n_my = A1[moves] + f_nb.sum(axis=1)      # (k,)
    n_opp = Ao[moves] - f_nb.sum(axis=1)     # (k,)

    # opp2 = opponent cells not flipped; Aob = their neighbour counts
    opp2 = opp[None, :] & ~flips             # (k, N)
    Aob = opp2.astype(np.int64) @ adjacency.astype(np.int64)  # (k, N)

    threat = empty[None, :] & adj_c & (Aob > 0) & (n_opp[:, None] + 1 >= n_my[:, None])

    tcount = np.minimum(threat.sum(axis=1), 2).astype(np.float64)
    value = -(points[moves].astype(np.float64) / 5.0) * (tcount / 2.0)
    return value

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Sum over empty cells at graph distance 2 from the candidate of points / (1 + opponent pressure), i.e. two-step reach discounted by how contested it is, divided by 30."""
    N = owner.shape[0]
    E = (owner == 0)
    opp = (owner == -1)
    A = adjacency.astype(np.float64)
    Ao = A @ opp.astype(np.float64)  # opponent neighbours per cell
    pts = points.astype(np.float64)
    # two-step reach: empty cells two hops from candidate (vectorised)
    A_moves = adjacency[moves].astype(np.float64)  # (k, N)
    reach1 = A_moves * E[None, :]
    reach2 = (reach1 @ A) * E[None, :]
    reach2 = reach2 * (1.0 - A_moves)  # exclude distance-1 cells
    # discount each two-step cell by opponent pressure (1/(1+count))
    discount = (1.0 / (1.0 + Ao))[None, :]
    values = (reach2 * discount * pts[None, :]).sum(axis=1) / 30.0
    return values
feature.measures: Sum over empty cells at graph distance 2 from the candidate of points / (1 + opponent pressure), i.e. two-step reach discounted by how contested it is, divided by 30.

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Net flip balance spread over the opponent's best reply: points I would flip now minus the points the opponent's single best flip-back could take, scaled by how much of the game is left, /15."""
    N = owner.shape[0]
    mine = (owner == 1)
    opp = (owner == -1)
    empty = (owner == 0)
    A1 = adjacency @ mine.astype(np.int64)
    Ao = adjacency @ opp.astype(np.int64)
    pts = points.astype(np.float64)
    my_home = homes[0]
    opp_home = homes[1]
    not_my_home = np.ones(N, dtype=bool); not_my_home[my_home] = False
    not_opp_home = np.ones(N, dtype=bool); not_opp_home[opp_home] = False

    adj_moves = adjacency[moves]
    is_opp = opp[None, :] & not_opp_home[None, :]
    flip = adj_moves & is_opp & (A1[None, :] + 1 >= Ao[None, :])
    gain = (flip * pts[None, :]).sum(1)

    A1b = A1[None, :] + adj_moves.astype(np.int64) + flip.astype(np.int64) @ adjacency.astype(np.int64)
    Aob = Ao[None, :] - flip.astype(np.int64) @ adjacency.astype(np.int64)

    legal_e = empty[None, :] & (Aob > 0) & ~adj_moves
    adj_j = adjacency[None, :, :]
    mymask = (mine & not_my_home)[None, None, :]
    cond_j = (Aob[:, None, :] + 1 >= A1b[:, None, :])
    fb = legal_e[:, :, None] & adj_j & mymask & cond_j
    loss_per_e = (fb * pts[None, None, :]).sum(2)
    loss = loss_per_e.max(1)

    # spread: how many distinct empty cells offer a profitable flip-back (0..3), as a "breadth" measure
    profitable = (loss_per_e > 0).sum(1).astype(np.float64)
    breadth = np.minimum(profitable, 3.0) / 3.0

    # remaining-game weighting: early claims are less costly to expose than late ones
    remaining = max(N - 2 - turn, 0)
    frac = remaining / float(max(N - 2, 1))

    net = (gain - loss) / 15.0
    # amplify net when many flip-back options exist (opponent has choices), damp when game nearly over
    return net * (0.5 + 0.5 * breadth) * (0.3 + 0.7 * frac)
feature.measures: Net flip balance spread over the opponent's best reply: points I would flip now minus the points the opponent's single best flip-back could take, scaled by how much of the game is left, /15.

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Number of opponent cells adjacent to the candidate that are NOT flippable by it, minus flippable ones, weighted by their point value /15."""
    A1 = (adjacency & (owner == 1)[None, :]).sum(1)
    Ao = (adjacency & (owner == -1)[None, :]).sum(1)
    cand = adjacency[moves]
    opp_nb = cand & (owner == -1)[None, :]

    not_home = np.ones(owner.shape[0], dtype=bool)

    flippable = flippable & not_home[None, :]
    stubborn = opp_nb & ~flippable & not_home[None, :]
    pts = points[None, :].astype(float)
    val = (stubborn.astype(float) * pts).sum(1) - (flippable.astype(float) * pts).sum(1)

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Net swing in points from this claim's flips minus the value the opponent can flip straight back next turn from the emptied neighbourhood."""
    N = owner.shape[0]
    mine = (owner == 1)
    opp = (owner == -1)
    empty = (owner == 0)
    pts = points.astype(np.float64)
    idx = np.arange(N)

    A1 = adjacency @ mine.astype(np.int64)
    Ao = adjacency @ opp.astype(np.int64)

    adj_c = adjacency[moves]                                   # (k, N)
    not_opp_home = idx != homes[1]
    flippable = adj_c & opp[None, :] & not_opp_home[None, :] & (A1[None, :] + 1 >= Ao[None, :])

    # points gained by flipping
    gain = (flippable * pts[None, :]).sum(axis=1)

    # after my claim + flips: my count and opp count per opponent cell that remains
    flips_per_cell = flippable.sum(axis=0)                     # (N,) how many candidates flip cell j
    # per-candidate remaining opp cells with updated neighbour counts
    opp_rem = opp[None, :] & ~flippable                        # (k, N)
    A1b = A1[None, :] + flippable.astype(np.int64)             # my neighbours after flips (approx: +1 from claim only on c)
    # account for my new cell c contributing to its own neighbours
    A1b = A1b + adj_c.astype(np.int64)
    Aob = (opp_rem.astype(np.int64) @ adjacency.astype(np.int64))  # (k, N)

    # opponent's best recapture: for each candidate, look at empty cells e adjacent to remaining opp cells,
    # that opp could claim and then flip my cells j (not my home) with Aob[j]+1 >= A1b[j]
    my_rem = mine[None, :] | flippable                         # my cells (including newly flipped) per candidate
    not_my_home = idx != homes[0]
    # can-be-flipped-back mask depends on candidate via A1b/Aob
    back_flippable = my_rem & not_my_home[None, :] & ((Aob + 1) >= A1b)  # (k, N)

    # empty cells adjacent to remaining opp territory (opp can claim there)
    opp_frontier = empty[None, :] & (adj_c & opp_rem).any(axis=0)[None, :] & (opp_rem @ adjacency.astype(np.int64) > 0)
    # (k, N) : empty cell e that opp can claim now (adjacent to opp_rem)
    opp_legal = empty[None, :] & (opp_rem.astype(np.int64) @ adjacency.astype(np.int64) > 0)

    # loss from recapture: for each legal opp cell e, points[e] claimed + points of my cells it flips back
    back_pts = (back_flippable * pts[None, :])                          # (k, N) points at risk per my cell
    recapture_value = pts[None, :] + (adjacency.astype(np.float64) @ back_pts.T).T  # (k, N) value if e claimed
    big_neg = np.where(opp_legal, recapture_value, -1.0)
    worst = big_neg.max(axis=1)
    worst = np.maximum(worst, 0.0)

    return (gain - worst) / 15.0
feature.measures: Net swing in points from this claim's flips minus the value the opponent can flip straight back next turn from the emptied neighbourhood.

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Sum of points in the opponent-free connected pocket reachable from each candidate (0 if candidate not opponent-free), divided by 30."""
    N = owner.shape[0]
    E = (owner == 0)
    opp = (owner == -1)
    oppn = adjacency.astype(int) @ opp.astype(int)
    free = E & (oppn == 0)

    # reachability closure over `free` via repeated boolean matrix propagation
    # reach[i, j] = j reachable from i within `free` (including i itself if free)
    reach = free[:, None] & free[None, :] & adjacency
    # iterate until fixpoint (at most N steps)
    for _ in range(N):
        new_reach = reach | (reach.astype(int) @ reach.astype(int) > 0)
        if np.array_equal(new_reach, reach):
            break
        reach = new_reach
    # include self
    reach = reach | (free[:, None] & (np.arange(N)[None, :] == np.arange(N)[:, None]))

    pocket_points = reach.astype(float) @ points.astype(float)

    values = np.zeros(moves.shape[0], dtype=float)
    for i, c in enumerate(moves):
        if not free[c]:
            continue
        values[i] = pocket_points[c] / 30.0
    return values

system:
You are the **Navigator** in Helix, an evolutionary search. You don't write candidates. You keep the search oriented: you maintain a map of **approaches** (the different ways the incumbent could be improved) and decide where the effort goes next.

Two loops do the work. The **deep loop** (a Researcher, then Coders) runs experiments on the approaches you assign. The **wide loop** (a Mutator) makes undirected variations of whatever you hand it, and of nothing else: it never sees approaches or hypotheses, only artefacts and scores.

## The approach tree

Each approach has a state:
- `untried`: brainstormed, not tested yet;
- `promising`: something under it gained on validation. Gets the most effort, and is split into deeper sub-approaches;
- `unproven`: tried without a gain, but nothing shows it can't work. Retried occasionally, at lower priority. Bad scores are not proof;
- `pruned`: the engine verified a certificate that everything under it adds nothing. Never assigned again.

## Each generation, decide

1. **Brainstorm** new approaches when the map is thin or the promising ones are drying up. Make them genuinely different from each other, and add deeper sub-approaches under promising ones.
2. **Assign the Researcher** to approaches, each with a mode: `explore` (an untried approach), `exploit` (deepen a promising one), `probe` (a cheap experiment to learn whether an unproven one has anything).
3. **Hand the Mutator parents**: ids from the ledger to vary. The engine already gives two slots to the most important kept features (variants of kept features win far more often); you choose the rest. Spread those: width means variety across approaches. Near-misses and surprising scores are good parents.
4. **Combinations**: pairs of features that each gained on their own but weren't kept, to retry together (some things only help next to another). A pair with a member that showed no gain alone is skipped: in testing, such pairs never gained.
5. **Prune requests**: approaches you believe are dead. The Prover will try to certify it; only a verified certificate prunes.

Effort follows evidence, but keep a share for the unproven and the untried: a search that only exploits stops finding things.

## Reply format

Start with the JSON block, then at most 80 words on your reasoning.

```json
{"new_approaches": [{"title": "<short>", "description": "<one sentence>", "parent": "<approach id or empty>"}],
 "research": [{"approach": "<id, or the exact title of a new approach>", "mode": "explore | exploit | probe", "why": "<one line>"}],
 "mutate": {"vary": ["<id>", "..."], "fresh": <how many fresh slots>},
 "combine": [["<id>", "<id>"]],
 "prune": ["<approach id>"]}
```

## What a candidate is here: a feature

The incumbent is a policy, a weighted sum of features; approaches are kinds of measurements (what quantity, under which conditions). Mutator parents are feature ids.

# The problem: Duel: play an invented territory game against a pool of scripted opponents

Play an invented two-player board game, "spore", against a fixed pool of scripted opponents. The policy is one player; it chooses its move each turn.

**The board.** A connected graph of about 30 cells. Each cell is worth 1, 2 or 5 points (about 60% are worth 1, 25% worth 2, 15% worth 5). Each player starts owning one *home* cell (worth 1); the two homes are far apart. All other cells start empty.

**A turn.** Players alternate. On your turn you must *claim* one empty cell that is adjacent to at least one cell you own; it becomes yours. Then *flips*: every opponent cell adjacent to the cell you just claimed (except the opponent's home, which never flips) becomes yours if, counting after your claim, you own at least as many of its neighbours as its owner does. Flips are decided all at once from the board right after the claim and do not chain: a flipped cell does not trigger further flips. A player with no legal claim (no empty cell next to its cells) passes and the other player continues.

**The end.** The game ends when no empty cell is left (about 30 claims in all, roughly half of them yours). Each player scores the points of the cells it owns at the end.

**One decision** = choosing which cell to claim. The **candidates** are your legal claims, in a random order (cells are also numbered at random). When there is only one legal claim it is taken automatically.

**Instances and cost.** An instance is 24 games on freshly generated boards of one family: 6 against each of the 4 opponents in the pool, moving first in half of them. The opponents are scripted players with different, fixed behaviour; their logic and identity are hidden, and you never see their future moves. The instance's **cost** is 100 x the opponents' share of all points scored in its games (in [0, 100]; the board's points are always all claimed). The **gap** is 100 x cost / the cost of Code Zero (the policy that always takes the first candidate, i.e. a random legal claim) on the same instance: Code Zero scores 100, lower is better. An opponent always keeps at least its home, so 0 is impossible; there is no known best.

Three training families, differing in board shape: `grid` (a 6 x 6 square grid, 4 random cells removed, 4 neighbours per cell), `hex` (a 6 x 5 hexagonal grid, 2 cells removed, up to 6 neighbours) and `web` (32 random points, each joined to its 3 nearest). The test split adds a board shape that training never shows.

## A feature

```python
import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """One line: exactly what this measures."""
    ...
    return values   # one number per candidate
```

- `moves`: shape (k,), int: the cells you may claim (the candidates), in random order. Index into the per-cell arrays below.
- `owner`: shape (N,), int8: for every cell on the board: 1 = yours, -1 = the opponent's, 0 = empty (N = number of cells).
- `homes`: shape (2,), int: your home cell and the opponent's home cell (homes never flip).
- `points`: shape (N,), int: what each cell is worth (1, 2 or 5).
- `adjacency`: shape (N, N), bool: which cells are neighbours (symmetric, False on the diagonal).
- `turn`: int: how many claims (by both players) have been made so far in this game; the game lasts N - 2 claims.
- Your current score is `points[owner == 1].sum()`, the opponent's `points[owner == -1].sum()`.
- Return one finite number per candidate (shape (k,)), or a few columns (shape (k, c)). The highest-scoring candidate is claimed.
- Import only `numpy` and `math`. No state between calls, no randomness, don't modify the inputs, no Python loops over candidates when a vectorised form exists (features run thousands of times per evaluation). Guard every division and log.
- Return finite numbers, roughly in [-1, 1] (normalise; the optimiser rescales anyway).

## How the policy works

priority(candidate) = w1 * feature1 + w2 * feature2 + ...; the highest priority wins; on a tie, the first candidate wins. With no features every candidate scores 0, so the first candidate always wins: that is **Code Zero**, the starting point (0% progress). An optimiser fits the weights, including their signs. A new feature is kept only if the policy does better with it than the same refit without it, on training instances *and* on separate validation instances, and the gain isn't already given by the kept features.

## How policies are scored

Per instance, the **gap** is how far the solution is above a reference (lower is better). The score is the mean gap over families. **Progress** is the share of the way from Code Zero (0%) to the best reachable (100%).

# The problem: Duel: play an invented territory game against a pool of scripted opponents

Play an invented two-player board game, "spore", against a fixed pool of scripted opponents. The policy is one player; it chooses its move each turn.

**The board.** A connected graph of about 30 cells. Each cell is worth 1, 2 or 5 points (about 60% are worth 1, 25% worth 2, 15% worth 5). Each player starts owning one *home* cell (worth 1); the two homes are far apart. All other cells start empty.

**A turn.** Players alternate. On your turn you must *claim* one empty cell that is adjacent to at least one cell you own; it becomes yours. Then *flips*: every opponent cell adjacent to the cell you just claimed (except the opponent's home, which never flips) becomes yours if, counting after your claim, you own at least as many of its neighbours as its owner does. Flips are decided all at once from the board right after the claim and do not chain: a flipped cell does not trigger further flips. A player with no legal claim (no empty cell next to its cells) passes and the other player continues.

**The end.** The game ends when no empty cell is left (about 30 claims in all, roughly half of them yours). Each player scores the points of the cells it owns at the end.

**One decision** = choosing which cell to claim. The **candidates** are your legal claims, in a random order (cells are also numbered at random). When there is only one legal claim it is taken automatically.

**Instances and cost.** An instance is 24 games on freshly generated boards of one family: 6 against each of the 4 opponents in the pool, moving first in half of them. The opponents are scripted players with different, fixed behaviour; their logic and identity are hidden, and you never see their future moves. The instance's **cost** is 100 x the opponents' share of all points scored in its games (in [0, 100]; the board's points are always all claimed). The **gap** is 100 x cost / the cost of Code Zero (the policy that always takes the first candidate, i.e. a random legal claim) on the same instance: Code Zero scores 100, lower is better. An opponent always keeps at least its home, so 0 is impossible; there is no known best.

Three training families, differing in board shape: `grid` (a 6 x 6 square grid, 4 random cells removed, 4 neighbours per cell), `hex` (a 6 x 5 hexagonal grid, 2 cells removed, up to 6 neighbours) and `web` (32 random points, each joined to its 3 nearest). The test split adds a board shape that training never shows.

Play an invented two-player board game, "spore", against a fixed pool of scripted opponents. The policy is one player; it chooses its move each turn.

**The board.** A connected graph of about 30 cells. Each cell is worth 1, 2 or 5 points (about 60% are worth 1, 25% worth 2, 15% worth 5). Each player starts owning one *home* cell (worth 1); the two homes are far apart. All other cells start empty.

**A turn.** Players alternate. On your turn you must *claim* one empty cell that is adjacent to at least one cell you own; it becomes yours. **The end.** The game ends when no empty cell is left (about 30 claims in all, roughly half of them yours). Each player scores the points of the cells it owns at the end.

**One decision** = choosing which cell to claim. The **candidates** are your legal claims, in a random order (cells are also numbered at random). When there is only one legal claim it is taken automatically.

You are the **Researcher** in Helix, an evolutionary search. You are the deep loop: you work out *why* the current best candidate loses where it does, and you design experiments that find out. The Mutator, another agent, makes undirected variations; you cash in on what it stumbles on and on what your own experiments reveal.

## What you get

- the incumbent (the current best) and its parts: what each part actually does and how much the result relies on it;
- **diagnostics**: named metrics of the incumbent's results, next to a reference where one exists. This is where the mechanism shows;
- **sensitivity probes**: each part of the incumbent knocked out, weakened and amplified. A gain from amplifying means a direction is under-used; a loss from weakening means the incumbent relies on it;
- the **ledger** for the approaches you're assigned: what was tried, how it scored, and whether its prediction held;
- the **Mutator's recent finds**: things that scored well or nearly well without anyone knowing why. Explaining and sharpening a lucky find is often the best experiment available;
- your **assignments** from the Navigator: which approaches to work on, and how (explore a new one, exploit a promising one, probe a doubtful one).

## How to work

1. **Find a mechanism, not a symptom.** Name a concrete difference between the incumbent's results and the reference (or between what works and what doesn't), and the decision that produces it.
2. **Design experiments of two kinds:**
   - `probe`: written to *learn*. Change one thing, or exaggerate one aspect, so the result tells you whether that aspect matters. Judged by whether its prediction held, not by its score.
   - `improve`: written to *win*.
3. **Don't repeat the ledger.** If an idea was tried, change it meaningfully or leave it. A disguised copy is detected and discarded. When the ledger shows a group of tried features that behave alike, that idea is spent: look at a different quantity altogether.
4. **Learn from what failed.** A prediction that didn't hold means the mechanism you believed is wrong or incomplete. Say what it taught you (`lesson`) before proposing the next experiment.
5. **Predict.** Every experiment names one metric from the diagnostics, where it should move (a family or scope), and the direction. The engine checks it.
6. **Be exact** in `change`: describe the candidate so precisely that it can be written without guessing.

## What a candidate is here: a feature

The incumbent is a policy: a weighted sum of **features** (measurements of a candidate in one decision). An optimiser fits the weights and their signs, so never choose numbers or signs: choose *what to measure*. The parts in the sensitivity probes are the kept features; amplifying one means multiplying its weight.

- `change` is the exact measurement, per candidate, in terms of the arguments, so a Coder can write it without guessing. Say what it is for the last or special candidates when that matters.

# The problem: Duel: play an invented territory game against a pool of scripted opponents

Play an invented two-player board game, "spore", against a fixed pool of scripted opponents. The policy is one player; it chooses its move each turn.

**The board.** A connected graph of about 30 cells. Each cell is worth 1, 2 or 5 points (about 60% are worth 1, 25% worth 2, 15% worth 5). Each player starts owning one *home* cell (worth 1); the two homes are far apart. All other cells start empty.

**A turn.** Players alternate. On your turn you must *claim* one empty cell that is adjacent to at least one cell you own; it becomes yours. Then *flips*: every opponent cell adjacent to the cell you just claimed (except the opponent's home, which never flips) becomes yours if, counting after your claim, you own at least as many of its neighbours as its owner does. Flips are decided all at once from the board right after the claim and do not chain: a flipped cell does not trigger further flips. A player with no legal claim (no empty cell next to its cells) passes and the other player continues.

**The end.** The game ends when no empty cell is left (about 30 claims in all, roughly half of them yours). Each player scores the points of the cells it owns at the end.

**One decision** = choosing which cell to claim. The **candidates** are your legal claims, in a random order (cells are also numbered at random). When there is only one legal claim it is taken automatically.

**Instances and cost.** An instance is 24 games on freshly generated boards of one family: 6 against each of the 4 opponents in the pool, moving first in half of them. The opponents are scripted players with different, fixed behaviour; their logic and identity are hidden, and you never see their future moves. The instance's **cost** is 100 x the opponents' share of all points scored in its games (in [0, 100]; the board's points are always all claimed). The **gap** is 100 x cost / the cost of Code Zero (the policy that always takes the first candidate, i.e. a random legal claim) on the same instance: Code Zero scores 100, lower is better. An opponent always keeps at least its home, so 0 is impossible; there is no known best.

Three training families, differing in board shape: `grid` (a 6 x 6 square grid, 4 random cells removed, 4 neighbours per cell), `hex` (a 6 x 5 hexagonal grid, 2 cells removed, up to 6 neighbours) and `web` (32 random points, each joined to its 3 nearest). The test split adds a board shape that training never shows.

# The problem: Duel: play an invented territory game against a pool of scripted opponents

Play an invented two-player board game, "spore", against a fixed pool of scripted opponents. The policy is one player; it chooses its move each turn.

**The board.** A connected graph of about 30 cells. Each cell is worth 1, 2 or 5 points (about 60% are worth 1, 25% worth 2, 15% worth 5). Each player starts owning one *home* cell (worth 1); the two homes are far apart. All other cells start empty.

**A turn.** Players alternate. On your turn you must *claim* one empty cell that is adjacent to at least one cell you own; it becomes yours. Then *flips*: every opponent cell adjacent to the cell you just claimed (except the opponent's home, which never flips) becomes yours if, counting after your claim, you own at least as many of its neighbours as its owner does. Flips are decided all at once from the board right after the claim and do not chain: a flipped cell does not trigger further flips. A player with no legal claim (no empty cell next to its cells) passes and the other player continues.

**The end.** The game ends when no empty cell is left (about 30 claims in all, roughly half of them yours). Each player scores the points of the cells it owns at the end.

**One decision** = choosing which cell to claim. The **candidates** are your legal claims, in a random order (cells are also numbered at random). When there is only one legal claim it is taken automatically.

**Instances and cost.** An instance is 24 games on freshly generated boards of one family: 6 against each of the 4 opponents in the pool, moving first in half of them. The opponents are scripted players with different, fixed behaviour; their logic and identity are hidden, and you never see their future moves. The instance's **cost** is 100 x the opponents' share of all points scored in its games (in [0, 100]; the board's points are always all claimed). The **gap** is 100 x cost / the cost of Code Zero (the policy that always takes the first candidate, i.e. a random legal claim) on the same instance: Code Zero scores 100, lower is better. An opponent always keeps at least its home, so 0 is impossible; there is no known best.

Three training families, differing in board shape: `grid` (a 6 x 6 square grid, 4 random cells removed, 4 neighbours per cell), `hex` (a 6 x 5 hexagonal grid, 2 cells removed, up to 6 neighbours) and `web` (32 random points, each joined to its 3 nearest). The test split adds a board shape that training never shows.

## How the policy works

priority(candidate) = w1 * feature1 + w2 * feature2 + ...; the highest priority wins; on a tie, the first candidate wins. With no features every candidate scores 0, so the first candidate always wins: that is **Code Zero**, the starting point (0% progress). An optimiser fits the weights, including their signs. ## How policies are scored

Per instance, the **gap** is how far the solution is above a reference (lower is better). The score is the mean gap over families. **Progress** is the share of the way from Code Zero (0%) to the best reachable (100%).

```python
import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """(points of empty neighbours with no opponent neighbour minus points of empty neighbours with an opponent neighbour) / 15."""
    opp = (owner == -1).astype(np.float64)
    Ao = adjacency @ opp  # (N,) count of opponent neighbours per cell
    nb = adjacency[moves] & (owner == 0)[None, :]  # (k, N) empty neighbours of each candidate
    contested = nb & (Ao > 0)[None, :]
    exclusive = nb & (Ao == 0)[None, :]
    p = points.astype(np.float64)
    return ((p * exclusive).sum(axis=1) - (p * contested).sum(axis=1)) / 15.0
```

This computes, for each candidate, the point value of its empty neighbours that have no opponent neighbour minus the point value of its empty neighbours that do have an opponent neighbour, divided by 15; I read "contested" as empty neighbours adjacent to at least one opponent-owned cell, exactly as specified.

```python
import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Exclusive 5-point-cell access race: sum over 5-point empty cells j of 5/(1+D[c,j]) for D<=3 and D<d_opp[j], /15, only when no candidate can flip anything."""
    N = owner.shape[0]
    k = moves.shape[0]
    empty = (owner == 0)
    opp = (owner == -1)
    mine = (owner == 1)

    # Opponent adjacency counts (Ao) and my adjacency counts (A1) per cell.
    Ao = adjacency @ opp.astype(np.int32)
    A1 = adjacency @ mine.astype(np.int32)

    # Flippable pairs: opponent non-home cells adjacent to a candidate with A1+1 >= Ao.
    opp_home = homes[1]
    nonhome_opp = opp.copy()
    nonhome_opp[opp_home] = False
    # For each candidate c, count opponent non-home neighbours that would flip.
    # A cell x flips if adjacency[c,x] and nonhome_opp[x] and A1[x]+1 >= Ao[x].
    flippable_cell = nonhome_opp & ((A1 + 1) >= Ao)
    # candidates adjacent to any flippable cell
    adj_to_flippable = adjacency[:, flippable_cell].any(axis=1) if flippable_cell.any() else np.zeros(N, dtype=bool)
    total_flippable = int(adj_to_flippable[moves].sum())

    if total_flippable != 0:
        return np.zeros(k)

    # d_opp: BFS through empty cells only, starting from empty cells adjacent to opponent.
    d_opp = np.full(N, 99, dtype=np.int32)
    frontier = empty & (Ao > 0)
    d_opp[frontier] = 1
    for step in range(2, 5):
        # expand: empty cells adjacent to current frontier, not yet reached
        nbr = (adjacency @ frontier.astype(np.int32)) > 0
        new = empty & nbr & (d_opp == 99)
        d_opp[new] = step
        frontier = new
        if not new.any():
            break

    # 5-point empty cells
    five = empty & (points == 5)
    five_idx = np.where(five)[0]

    if five_idx.size == 0:
        return np.zeros(k)

    # D: per candidate BFS through empty cells, steps 1..3.
    # D shape (k, N)
    D = np.full((k, N), 99, dtype=np.int32)
    D[np.arange(k), moves] = 0
    frontier = np.zeros((k, N), dtype=bool)
    frontier[np.arange(k), moves] = True
    for step in range(1, 4):
        nbr = (frontier.astype(np.int32) @ adjacency.T) > 0  # (k, N)
        new = empty[None, :] & nbr & (D == 99)
        D[new] = step
        frontier = new
        if not new.any():
            break

    # value = sum_j 5/(1+D[:,j]) for D<=3 and D < d_opp[j]
    Dj = D[:, five_idx].astype(np.float64)  # (k, m)
    dopp_j = d_opp[five_idx].astype(np.float64)  # (m,)
    mask = (Dj <= 3) & (Dj < dopp_j[None, :])
    contrib = np.where(mask, 5.0 / (1.0 + Dj), 0.0)
    value = contrib.sum(axis=1) / 15.0
    return value
```

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Sum over cells flipped by this claim of points[j] * min(post-flip owner-neighbour margin, 3), /15."""
    moves = np.asarray(moves, dtype=int)
    adj = adjacency.astype(np.int32)
    opp = (owner == -1)
    mine = (owner == 1)
    opp_home = int(homes[1])

    # Neighbour counts before the claim
    A1 = adj @ mine.astype(np.int32)          # my neighbours per cell
    Ao = adj @ opp.astype(np.int32)           # opponent neighbours per cell

    # Candidate rows
    adj_c = adj[moves]                        # (k, N)
    A1_c = A1[moves]                          # (k,)
    Ao_c = Ao[moves]

    # Flipped set F: opponent cells adjacent to c, not opp home, with A1+1 >= Ao
    is_opp = opp[None, :] & (np.arange(adj.shape[0])[None, :] != opp_home)
    F = adj_c.astype(bool) & is_opp & ((A1_c[:, None] + 1) >= Ao_c[:, None])  # (k, N)
    Ff = F.astype(np.int32)

    # Post-flip neighbour counts
    # A1' = A1 + adj[c] + F@adjacency ; Ao' = Ao - F@adjacency
    A1p = A1[None, :] + adj_c + Ff @ adj
    Aop = Ao[None, :] - Ff @ adj

    margin = A1p - Aop                          # (k, N)
    margin_clipped = np.minimum(margin, 3).astype(np.float64)

    vals = (F.astype(np.float64) * points[None, :].astype(np.float64) * margin_clipped).sum(axis=1)
    return vals / 15.0

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Exclusive 5-point-cell access race: sum over 5-point empty cells j of 5/(1+D[c,j]) for D<=3 and D<d_opp[j], /15, only when no candidate can flip anything."""
    N = owner.shape[0]
    k = moves.shape[0]
    empty = (owner == 0)
    opp = (owner == -1)
    mine = (owner == 1)

    # Opponent adjacency counts (Ao) and my adjacency counts (A1) per cell.
    Ao = adjacency @ opp.astype(np.int32)
    A1 = adjacency @ mine.astype(np.int32)

    # Flippable pairs: opponent non-home cells adjacent to a candidate with A1+1 >= Ao.
    opp_home = homes[1]
    nonhome_opp = opp.copy()
    nonhome_opp[opp_home] = False
    # For each candidate c, count opponent non-home neighbours that would flip.
    # A cell x flips if adjacency[c,x] and nonhome_opp[x] and A1[x]+1 >= Ao[x].
    flippable_cell = nonhome_opp & ((A1 + 1) >= Ao)
    # candidates adjacent to any flippable cell
    adj_to_flippable = adjacency[:, flippable_cell].any(axis=1) if flippable_cell.any() else np.zeros(N, dtype=bool)
    total_flippable = int(adj_to_flippable[moves].sum())

    if total_flippable != 0:
        return np.zeros(k)

    # d_opp: BFS through empty cells only, starting from empty cells adjacent to opponent.
    d_opp = np.full(N, 99, dtype=np.int32)
    frontier = empty & (Ao > 0)
    d_opp[frontier] = 1
    for step in range(2, 5):
        # expand: empty cells adjacent to current frontier, not yet reached
        nbr = (adjacency @ frontier.astype(np.int32)) > 0
        new = empty & nbr & (d_opp == 99)
        d_opp[new] = step
        frontier = new
        if not new.any():
            break

    # 5-point empty cells
    five = empty & (points == 5)
    five_idx = np.where(five)[0]

    if five_idx.size == 0:
        return np.zeros(k)

    # D: per candidate BFS through empty cells, steps 1..3.
    # D shape (k, N)
    D = np.full((k, N), 99, dtype=np.int32)
    D[np.arange(k), moves] = 0
    frontier = np.zeros((k, N), dtype=bool)
    frontier[np.arange(k), moves] = True
    for step in range(1, 4):
        nbr = (frontier.astype(np.int32) @ adjacency.T) > 0  # (k, N)
        new = empty[None, :] & nbr & (D == 99)
        D[new] = step
        frontier = new
        if not new.any():
            break

    # value = sum_j 5/(1+D[:,j]) for D<=3 and D < d_opp[j]
    Dj = D[:, five_idx].astype(np.float64)  # (k, m)
    dopp_j = d_opp[five_idx].astype(np.float64)  # (m,)
    mask = (Dj <= 3) & (Dj < dopp_j[None, :])
    contrib = np.where(mask, 5.0 / (1.0 + Dj), 0.0)
    value = contrib.sum(axis=1) / 15.0
    return value

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Sum over opponent cells adjacent to the candidate of points * (my-neighbour surplus toward flip), i.e. how close each adjacent opponent cell is to flipping, weighted by value, /15."""
    A1 = (adjacency & (owner == 1)[None, :]).sum(1).astype(np.float64)
    Ao = (adjacency & (owner == -1)[None, :]).sum(1).astype(np.float64)
    cand = adjacency[moves]
    opp_nb = cand & (owner == -1)[None, :]
    # margin: A1+1 - Ao  (>=0 means flips).  Use a soft proximity: 1/(1+max(margin,0)) so
    # already-flipping (margin>=0) cells count fully and near-miss cells (margin<0) count partially.
    margin = (A1[None, :] + 1.0) - Ao[None, :]
    prox = np.where(margin >= 0.0, 1.0, 1.0 / (1.0 + (-margin)))
    w = opp_nb.astype(np.float64) * prox * points[None, :].astype(np.float64)
    w[:, homes[1]] = 0.0
    return w.sum(1) / 15.0

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Weighted margin (my minus opponent neighbours after the claim) over empty/enemy non-home neighbours, signed by whether the margin is on our side of flipping, normalised by weighted adjacency count."""
    mine = (owner == 1)
    theirs = (owner == -1)
    A1 = (adjacency & mine[None, :]).sum(1)
    Ao = (adjacency & theirs[None, :]).sum(1)
    cand_adj = adjacency[moves]
    margin = (A1[None, :] + cand_adj.astype(np.float64)) - Ao[None, :]
    relevant = ((owner == 0) | (owner == -1))
    relevant[homes[0]] = False
    relevant[homes[1]] = False
    w = points.astype(np.float64) * relevant.astype(np.float64)
    # nonlinearity: squashing the margin so that being safely above 0 matters little,
    # being just at the flip boundary matters a lot, being below matters negatively.
    # use tanh of margin, and emphasize the boundary crossings.
    squashed = np.tanh(margin)
    # also give extra weight to cells that are exactly at boundary (margin in {0,1}) since they are flip-flippable
    boundary = np.exp(-np.abs(margin - 0.5))
    weight = w[None, :] * (0.5 * squashed + 0.5 * boundary)
    num = (cand_adj.astype(np.float64) * weight).sum(1)
    den = (cand_adj.astype(np.float64) * w[None, :]).sum(1) + 1e-9
    return num / den
feature.measures: Weighted margin (my minus opponent neighbours after the claim) over empty/enemy non-home neighbours, signed by whether the margin is on our side of flipping, normalised by weighted adjacency count.

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """For each candidate: points of the opponent-free pocket it opens into, but only the part of that pocket that is strictly closer (in free-cell steps) to the candidate than to the opponent's nearest territory; divided by 30."""
    N = owner.shape[0]
    empty = (owner == 0)
    opp = (owner == -1)
    pts = points.astype(np.float64)
    A = adjacency

    # opponent distance (BFS over all cells, step cost 1) from opponent territory
    INF = float(N + 5)
    d_opp = np.full(N, INF)
    d_opp[opp] = 0.0
    frontier = opp.copy()
    step = 0
    while frontier.any():
        step += 1
        nb = (A @ frontier.astype(np.int64)) > 0
        nb &= (d_opp == INF)
        if not nb.any():
            break
        d_opp[nb] = step
        frontier = nb

    # free pocket cells: empty with no opponent neighbour (safe to walk into)
    Ao = A @ opp.astype(np.int64)
    free = empty & (Ao == 0)

    out = np.zeros(moves.shape[0], dtype=np.float64)
    idx_all = np.arange(N)
    for i, c in enumerate(moves):
        if not free[c]:
            continue
        # BFS over free cells starting from c, distance in free-steps
        dfree = np.full(N, INF)
        dfree[c] = 0.0
        frontier = np.zeros(N, dtype=bool)
        frontier[c] = True
        step = 0
        while frontier.any():
            step += 1
            nb = (A @ frontier.astype(np.int64)) > 0
            nb &= free & (dfree == INF)
            if not nb.any():
                break
            dfree[nb] = step
            frontier = nb
        # pocket cells: free cells reached, plus c itself
        in_pocket = (dfree < INF)
        # rival distance from c to that cell through open/empty graph (upper bound on opponent arrival)
        # opponent arrival to a pocket cell j: d_opp[j] (in open steps) ; we compare free-steps from c vs opp open-steps
        closer = in_pocket & (dfree < d_opp)
        # exclude the candidate cell itself from the mass (it is claimed, not a future gain)
        mass_mask = closer & (idx_all != c)
        out[i] = pts[mass_mask].sum() / 30.0
    return out

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Tempo-weighted value of cells the opponent can claim next turn (their best immediate flip-count), negative, normalised."""
    N = owner.shape[0]
    mine = (owner == 1)
    opp = (owner == -1)
    empty = (owner == 0)
    A1 = adjacency @ mine.astype(np.int64)
    Ao = adjacency @ opp.astype(np.int64)
    pts = points.astype(np.float64)

    # cells adjacent to my territory that could be flipped by an opponent claim
    not_opp_home = np.ones(N, dtype=bool)
    not_opp_home[homes[1]] = False
    my_flippable = mine & not_opp_home & (Ao + 1 >= A1)

    # empty cells the opponent could claim (adjacent to opp territory)
    opp_legal = empty & (Ao > 0)

    if not opp_legal.any():
        return np.zeros(moves.shape[0], dtype=np.float64)

    # For each opponent-legal empty cell e, the value it could grab: points[e] + points of my flippable neighbours
    flippable_pts = np.where(my_flippable, pts, 0.0)
    grab_value = pts + adjacency @ flippable_pts  # (N,)
    best_opp_grab = grab_value[opp_legal].max() if opp_legal.any() else 0.0

    # For each candidate: does claiming it reduce that best threat? Estimate post-claim best opp grab.
    out = np.empty(moves.shape[0], dtype=np.float64)
    for i, c in enumerate(moves):
        adj_c = adjacency[c]
        flips = adj_c & opp & not_opp_home & ((A1 + 1) >= Ao)

        opp2 = opp & ~flips
        A1b = adjacency @ mine2.astype(np.int64)
        Aob = adjacency @ opp2.astype(np.int64)
        empty2 = empty & ~(np.arange(N) == c)
        opp_legal2 = empty2 & (Aob > 0)
        if not opp_legal2.any():
            out[i] = best_opp_grab
            continue
        my_flip2 = mine2 & not_opp_home & (Aob + 1 >= A1b)
        fp2 = np.where(my_flip2, pts, 0.0)
        gv2 = pts + adjacency @ fp2
        out[i] = gv2[opp_legal2].max()
    return -(out - best_opp_grab) / 15.0

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Sum of points of empty opponent-reachable-only neighbours of each candidate, divided by 15."""
    empty = (owner == 0)
    opp_reach = empty & (adjacency @ (owner == -1).astype(np.int64) > 0)
    mine_reach = empty & (adjacency @ (owner == 1).astype(np.int64) > 0)

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Negative BFS distance from each candidate to the opponent's home, but weighted by the point value of the cells on that path's frontier: candidates whose short path to the enemy home runs through low-value empty cells are favoured (denial), normalised by N."""
    N = adjacency.shape[0]
    target = int(homes[1])
    dist = np.full(N, -1, dtype=np.int64)
    dist[target] = 0
    frontier = np.array([target], dtype=np.int64)
    while frontier.size > 0:
        nb = adjacency[frontier].any(axis=0)
        nb[dist >= 0] = False
        nxt = np.nonzero(nb)[0]
        dist[nxt] = dist[frontier].min() + 1
        frontier = nxt
    d = dist[moves].astype(np.float64)
    d[d < 0] = N
    # value of empty cells adjacent to each candidate, that lie on a shortest path toward opp home
    dist_all = dist.astype(np.float64)
    dist_all[dist_all < 0] = N
    # candidate's own distance to target
    dm = dist_all[moves]  # (k,)
    # for each candidate, average value of its empty neighbours that are closer to the target
    closer = (dist_all[None, :] < dm[:, None]) & (owner == 0)[None, :]
    nb_mask = adjacency[moves] & closer
    val = (nb_mask * points[None, :]).sum(1)
    cnt = nb_mask.sum(1)
    meanval = val / np.maximum(cnt, 1)
    # combine: favours being close (negative dist) and having low-value approach cells (denial of high-value path)
    return (-d / float(N)) * (0.5 + 0.5 * (1.0 - meanval / 5.0))
feature.measures: Negative BFS distance from each candidate to the opponent's home, but weighted by the point value of the cells on that path's frontier: candidates whose short path to the enemy home runs through low-value empty cells are favoured (denial), normalised by N.

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Negative total points of empty cells adjacent to opponent territory after my claim and its flips, divided by 30."""
    N = owner.shape[0]
    my_nb = (adjacency & (owner == 1)[None, :]).sum(axis=1)
    opp_nb = (adjacency & (owner == -1)[None, :]).sum(axis=1)

    opp_cells = owner == -1
    empty_cells = owner == 0

    values = np.empty(moves.shape[0], dtype=float)
    for i, c in enumerate(moves):
        # cells adjacent to candidate c that are opponent-owned and not the opponent home
        adj_c = adjacency[:, c]
        flippable = opp_cells & adj_c & (np.arange(N) != homes[1])
        flipped = flippable & (my_nb + 1 >= opp_nb)
        new_opp = opp_cells & ~flipped
        # empty cells (excluding c) adjacent to at least one new_opp cell
        frontier = empty_cells & ~(np.arange(N) == c) & (adjacency[:, new_opp].any(axis=1))
        values[i] = -points[frontier].sum() / 30.0
    return values

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Negative (normalised) best one-ply grab value available to the opponent after my claim and its flips."""
    N = owner.shape[0]
    my_home = homes[0]
    opp_home = homes[1]
    mine = (owner == 1)
    opp = (owner == -1)
    empty = (owner == 0)
    A1 = adjacency @ mine.astype(np.int64)
    Ao = adjacency @ opp.astype(np.int64)
    pts = points.astype(np.float64)

    out = np.zeros(moves.shape[0], dtype=np.float64)
    for idx in range(moves.shape[0]):
        c = moves[idx]
        # flips: opponent cells adjacent to c, not opp home, with A1[j]+1 >= Ao[j]
        adj_c = adjacency[c]
        flips = adj_c & opp & (np.arange(N) != opp_home) & ((A1 + 1) >= Ao)
        mine2 = mine.copy()
        mine2[c] = True
        mine2 |= flips
        opp2 = opp & ~flips
        A1b = adjacency @ mine2.astype(np.int64)
        Aob = adjacency @ opp2.astype(np.int64)
        legal_e = empty & (Aob > 0)
        if not legal_e.any():
            out[idx] = 0.0
            continue
        # gain[e] = points[e] + sum over j adjacent to e with mine2[j], j != my home, Aob[j]+1 >= A1b[j]
        flip_back_mask = mine2 & (np.arange(N) != my_home) & ((Aob + 1) >= A1b)
        flip_back_pts = np.where(flip_back_mask, pts, 0.0)
        # for each empty e: sum of flip_back_pts over neighbours
        gain = pts + adjacency @ flip_back_pts
        best = gain[legal_e].max()
        out[idx] = -best / 30.0
    return out

idea.hypothesis: f026 counts the *total* points left on the opponent's frontier after my claim; what actually hurts is the single best move they can make (grab value + the points it flips back). Measuring their best one-ply payoff, negated, targets the denial chain one step deeper than a frontier sum.

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Negative points of each candidate times the capped count of empty neighbours from which the opponent could claim and flip it next turn."""
    N = owner.shape[0]
    my = (owner == 1)
    opp = (owner == -1)
    empty = (owner == 0)
    opp_home = homes[1]

    A1 = adjacency @ my.astype(np.int64)      # my neighbours per cell
    Ao = adjacency @ opp.astype(np.int64)    # opponent neighbours per cell

    # opponent cells that would flip if I claim c (per candidate)
    # flips[j] = opp cell j adjacent to c, j != opp home, A1[j] + 1 >= Ao[j]
    adj_c = adjacency[moves]                 # (k, N)
    is_opp = opp[None, :]
    not_home = np.ones(N, dtype=bool)
    not_home[opp_home] = False
    flip_cond = (A1[None, :] + 1 >= Ao[None, :])
    flips = adj_c & is_opp & not_home[None, :] & flip_cond   # (k, N)

    f_nb = flips.astype(np.int64)            # (k, N) flipped neighbours of c

    n_my = A1[moves] + f_nb.sum(axis=1)      # (k,)
    n_opp = Ao[moves] - f_nb.sum(axis=1)     # (k,)

    # opp2 = opponent cells not flipped; Aob = their neighbour counts
    opp2 = opp[None, :] & ~flips             # (k, N)
    Aob = opp2.astype(np.int64) @ adjacency.astype(np.int64)  # (k, N)

    threat = empty[None, :] & adj_c & (Aob > 0) & (n_opp[:, None] + 1 >= n_my[:, None])

    tcount = np.minimum(threat.sum(axis=1), 2).astype(np.float64)
    value = -(points[moves].astype(np.float64) / 5.0) * (tcount / 2.0)
    return value

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Sum over opponent cells adjacent to the candidate of points * (my-neighbour surplus toward flip), i.e. how close each adjacent opponent cell is to flipping, weighted by value, /15."""
    A1 = (adjacency & (owner == 1)[None, :]).sum(1).astype(np.float64)
    Ao = (adjacency & (owner == -1)[None, :]).sum(1).astype(np.float64)
    cand = adjacency[moves]
    opp_nb = cand & (owner == -1)[None, :]
    # margin: A1+1 - Ao  (>=0 means flips).  Use a soft proximity: 1/(1+max(margin,0)) so
    # already-flipping (margin>=0) cells count fully and near-miss cells (margin<0) count partially.
    margin = (A1[None, :] + 1.0) - Ao[None, :]
    prox = np.where(margin >= 0.0, 1.0, 1.0 / (1.0 + (-margin)))
    w = opp_nb.astype(np.float64) * prox * points[None, :].astype(np.float64)
    w[:, homes[1]] = 0.0
    return w.sum(1) / 15.0
feature.measures: Sum over opponent cells adjacent to the candidate of points * (my-neighbour surplus toward flip), i.e. how close each adjacent opponent cell is to flipping, weighted by value, /15.

feature.code:
import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Weighted margin (my minus opponent neighbours after the claim) over empty/enemy non-home neighbours, signed by whether the margin is on our side of flipping, normalised by weighted adjacency count."""
    mine = (owner == 1)
    theirs = (owner == -1)
    A1 = (adjacency & mine[None, :]).sum(1)
    Ao = (adjacency & theirs[None, :]).sum(1)
    cand_adj = adjacency[moves]
    margin = (A1[None, :] + cand_adj.astype(np.float64)) - Ao[None, :]
    relevant = ((owner == 0) | (owner == -1))
    relevant[homes[0]] = False
    relevant[homes[1]] = False
    w = points.astype(np.float64) * relevant.astype(np.float64)
    # nonlinearity: squashing the margin so that being safely above 0 matters little,
    # being just at the flip boundary matters a lot, being below matters negatively.
    # use tanh of margin, and emphasize the boundary crossings.
    squashed = np.tanh(margin)
    # also give extra weight to cells that are exactly at boundary (margin in {0,1}) since they are flip-flippable
    boundary = np.exp(-np.abs(margin - 0.5))
    weight = w[None, :] * (0.5 * squashed + 0.5 * boundary)
    num = (cand_adj.astype(np.float64) * weight).sum(1)
    den = (cand_adj.astype(np.float64) * w[None, :]).sum(1) + 1e-9
    return num / den
feature.measures: Weighted margin (my minus opponent neighbours after the claim) over empty/enemy non-home neighbours, signed by whether the margin is on our side of flipping, normalised by weighted adjacency count.

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """For each candidate: points of the opponent-free pocket it opens into, but only the part of that pocket that is strictly closer (in free-cell steps) to the candidate than to the opponent's nearest territory; divided by 30."""
    N = owner.shape[0]
    empty = (owner == 0)
    opp = (owner == -1)
    pts = points.astype(np.float64)
    A = adjacency

    # opponent distance (BFS over all cells, step cost 1) from opponent territory
    INF = float(N + 5)
    d_opp = np.full(N, INF)
    d_opp[opp] = 0.0
    frontier = opp.copy()
    step = 0
    while frontier.any():
        step += 1
        nb = (A @ frontier.astype(np.int64)) > 0
        nb &= (d_opp == INF)
        if not nb.any():
            break
        d_opp[nb] = step
        frontier = nb

    # free pocket cells: empty with no opponent neighbour (safe to walk into)
    Ao = A @ opp.astype(np.int64)
    free = empty & (Ao == 0)

    out = np.zeros(moves.shape[0], dtype=np.float64)
    idx_all = np.arange(N)
    for i, c in enumerate(moves):
        if not free[c]:
            continue
        # BFS over free cells starting from c, distance in free-steps
        dfree = np.full(N, INF)
        dfree[c] = 0.0
        frontier = np.zeros(N, dtype=bool)
        frontier[c] = True
        step = 0
        while frontier.any():
            step += 1
            nb = (A @ frontier.astype(np.int64)) > 0
            nb &= free & (dfree == INF)
            if not nb.any():
                break
            dfree[nb] = step
            frontier = nb
        # pocket cells: free cells reached, plus c itself
        in_pocket = (dfree < INF)
        # rival distance from c to that cell through open/empty graph (upper bound on opponent arrival)
        # opponent arrival to a pocket cell j: d_opp[j] (in open steps) ; we compare free-steps from c vs opp open-steps
        closer = in_pocket & (dfree < d_opp)
        # exclude the candidate cell itself from the mass (it is claimed, not a future gain)
        mass_mask = closer & (idx_all != c)
        out[i] = pts[mass_mask].sum() / 30.0
    return out
feature.measures: For each candidate: points of the opponent-free pocket it opens into, but only the part of that pocket that is strictly closer (in free-cell steps) to the candidate than to the opponent's nearest territory; divided by 30.

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Tempo-weighted value of cells the opponent can claim next turn (their best immediate flip-count), negative, normalised."""
    N = owner.shape[0]
    mine = (owner == 1)
    opp = (owner == -1)
    empty = (owner == 0)
    A1 = adjacency @ mine.astype(np.int64)
    Ao = adjacency @ opp.astype(np.int64)
    pts = points.astype(np.float64)

    # cells adjacent to my territory that could be flipped by an opponent claim
    not_opp_home = np.ones(N, dtype=bool)
    not_opp_home[homes[1]] = False
    my_flippable = mine & not_opp_home & (Ao + 1 >= A1)

    # empty cells the opponent could claim (adjacent to opp territory)
    opp_legal = empty & (Ao > 0)

    if not opp_legal.any():
        return np.zeros(moves.shape[0], dtype=np.float64)

    # For each opponent-legal empty cell e, the value it could grab: points[e] + points of my flippable neighbours
    flippable_pts = np.where(my_flippable, pts, 0.0)
    grab_value = pts + adjacency @ flippable_pts  # (N,)
    best_opp_grab = grab_value[opp_legal].max() if opp_legal.any() else 0.0

    # For each candidate: does claiming it reduce that best threat? Estimate post-claim best opp grab.
    out = np.empty(moves.shape[0], dtype=np.float64)
    for i, c in enumerate(moves):
        adj_c = adjacency[c]
        flips = adj_c & opp & not_opp_home & ((A1 + 1) >= Ao)
        mine2 = mine.copy(); mine2[c] = True; mine2 |= flips
        opp2 = opp & ~flips
        A1b = adjacency @ mine2.astype(np.int64)
        Aob = adjacency @ opp2.astype(np.int64)
        empty2 = empty & ~(np.arange(N) == c)
        opp_legal2 = empty2 & (Aob > 0)
        if not opp_legal2.any():
            out[i] = best_opp_grab
            continue
        my_flip2 = mine2 & not_opp_home & (Aob + 1 >= A1b)
        fp2 = np.where(my_flip2, pts, 0.0)
        gv2 = pts + adjacency @ fp2
        out[i] = gv2[opp_legal2].max()
    return -(out - best_opp_grab) / 15.0
feature.measures: Tempo-weighted value of cells the opponent can claim next turn (their best immediate flip-count), negative, normalised.

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Negative count (over empty cells) of opponent claims that would flip at least one of my cells after my claim, divided by N."""
    N = owner.shape[0]
    mine = (owner == 1)
    opp = (owner == -1)
    empty = (owner == 0)
    opp_home = homes[1]

    A1 = adjacency @ mine.astype(np.int64)
    Ao = adjacency @ opp.astype(np.int64)

    k = moves.shape[0]
    out = np.zeros(k, dtype=np.float64)

    adj = adjacency.astype(np.int64)
    adj_moves = adj[moves]  # (k, N)

    for idx in range(k):
        c = moves[idx]
        # F: opponent cells adjacent to c, excluding opponent home, with A1+1 >= Ao
        cand_opp = adj[c] & opp
        cand_opp[opp_home] = False
        F = cand_opp & ((A1 + 1) >= Ao)

        A1p = A1 + adj[c] + (F.astype(np.int64) @ adj)
        Aop = Ao - (F.astype(np.int64) @ adj)

        mineMask = mine | (np.arange(N) == c) | F

        # For each empty cell e: does there exist j in mineMask with Aop[j] + adj[e,j] >= A1p[j]?
        # i.e. opponent claiming e would flip j.
        # Condition per (e, j): mineMask[j] and Aop[j] + adj[e,j] >= A1p[j]
        # adj[e,j] is 1 if e adjacent j. So need Aop[j] + 1 >= A1p[j] for adjacent j,
        # or Aop[j] >= A1p[j] for non-adjacent j (but e must be adjacent to claim, so only adjacent matters).
        # Opponent can claim e only if e is adjacent to opponent territory (Ao'[e] >= 1).
        # Aop[e] >= 1 means e adjacent to some opponent cell.
        # For flip: exists j in mineMask adjacent to e with Aop[j] + 1 >= A1p[j].
        # (Aop[j] + adj[e,j] >= A1p[j]; adj[e,j]=1 for adjacent j.)
        # j must be adjacent to e to be flipped by claiming e.
        # So: for each e, check if any neighbor j of e has mineMask[j] and Aop[j]+1 >= A1p[j].
        # Vectorize: build matrix over (e, j) where e empty, j neighbor.
        # flip_ok[j] = mineMask[j] & (Aop[j] + 1 >= A1p[j])
        flip_ok = mineMask & ((Aop + 1) >= A1p)
        # For each empty e: any neighbor j with flip_ok[j]
        # adj[e] & flip_ok -> any
        # adj is (N,N); adj[e] row gives neighbors of e
        # (adj @ flip_ok.astype(int)) > 0 gives for each e whether any neighbor j has flip_ok
        has_flip_neighbor = (adj @ flip_ok.astype(np.int64)) > 0
        # e must be empty and opponent-reachable (Aop[e] >= 1)
        valid_e = empty & (Aop >= 1) & has_flip_neighbor
        out[idx] = -np.count_nonzero(valid_e) / N

    return out

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """(points of empty neighbours with no opponent neighbour minus points of empty neighbours with an opponent neighbour) / 15."""
    opp = (owner == -1).astype(np.float64)
    Ao = adjacency @ opp  # (N,) count of opponent neighbours per cell
    nb = adjacency[moves] & (owner == 0)[None, :]  # (k, N) empty neighbours of each candidate
    contested = nb & (Ao > 0)[None, :]
    exclusive = nb & (Ao == 0)[None, :]
    p = points.astype(np.float64)
    return ((p * exclusive).sum(axis=1) - (p * contested).sum(axis=1)) / 15.0
