import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Opponent cells adjacent to the candidate, weighted by points and by how exposed they are to a *future* flip (already-flipping cells discounted, since f006 handles them), using the opponent cell's own degree as a normaliser so high-degree enemy cells are harder to crack, /15."""
    A1 = (adjacency & (owner == 1)[None, :]).sum(1).astype(np.float64)
    Ao = (adjacency & (owner == -1)[None, :]).sum(1).astype(np.float64)
    deg = adjacency.sum(1).astype(np.float64)
    cand = adjacency[moves]
    opp_nb = cand & (owner == -1)[None, :]
    # margin: how far each adjacent opp cell is from flipping after this claim
    margin = (A1[None, :] + 1.0) - Ao[None, :]
    # already-flipping (margin>=0) -> 0 (f006 covers those); near-miss (margin<0) -> partial credit
    # scaled by how many neighbours that opp cell has: a high-degree cell has more slack.
    slack = np.maximum(deg[None, :] - Ao[None, :], 1.0)
    prox = np.where(margin >= 0.0, 0.0, 1.0 / (1.0 + (-margin)))
    w = opp_nb.astype(np.float64) * prox * points[None, :].astype(np.float64) / slack
    w[:, homes[1]] = 0.0
    return w.sum(1) / 15.0

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Fraction of the candidate's neighbours that are empty and also adjacent to me, minus the same fraction for opponent-adjacent empties: how much this claim advances into a region only I can reach."""
    N = owner.shape[0]
    mine = (owner == 1).astype(np.int64)
    opp = (owner == -1).astype(np.int64)
    empty = (owner == 0)
    A1 = adjacency @ mine
    Ao = adjacency @ opp
    cand_nb = adjacency[moves]                       # (k, N)
    nb_count = cand_nb.sum(1).astype(np.float64)
    nb_count = np.maximum(nb_count, 1.0)
    # empty neighbours of candidate that I can already reach (contiguous expansion)
    mine_only = cand_nb & empty[None, :] & (A1[None, :] > 0)
    opp_touch = cand_nb & empty[None, :] & (Ao[None, :] > 0)
    f_mine = mine_only.sum(1).astype(np.float64) / nb_count
    f_opp = opp_touch.sum(1).astype(np.float64) / nb_count
    return f_mine - f_opp
feature.measures: Fraction of the candidate's neighbours that are empty and also adjacent to me, minus the same fraction for opponent-adjacent empties: how much this claim advances into a region only I can reach.

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Sum over opponent neighbours j of c of points[j] * convertibility[j,c] / (1 + deficit[j]), /15, where convertibility counts only empty neighbours e of j that are NOT already supported by my territory but become supported by claiming c (the follow-through claim exists)."""
    N = owner.shape[0]
    mine = (owner == 1)
    theirs = (owner == -1)
    empty = (owner == 0)

    A1 = (adjacency & mine[None, :]).sum(axis=1).astype(np.float64)   # my neighbours per cell
    Ao = (adjacency & theirs[None, :]).sum(axis=1).astype(np.float64)  # opp neighbours per cell

    cand = adjacency[moves]                       # (k, N)
    opp_nb = cand & theirs[None, :]               # (k, N)
    opp_nb[:, homes[1]] = False

    # deficit: extra my-supporters still needed after claiming c
    d = np.maximum(0.0, Ao - A1 - 1.0)            # (N,)

    # Only count empty neighbours e of j that are NOT already supported by my territory
    # but ARE adjacent to c: these are the genuine follow-through claims that convert j.
    base_sup = (A1 > 0)                           # (N,)
    empty_f = empty.astype(np.float64)
    base_f = base_sup.astype(np.float64)
    unsup_empty = empty_f * (1.0 - base_f)        # (N,)

    # conv[j,k] = # empty neighbours e of j with unsup_empty[e] and adjacency[moves[k], e]
    weighted_adj = adjacency * unsup_empty[None, :]   # (N, N)
    conv = weighted_adj @ cand.T.astype(np.float64)   # (N, k)

    weight = (opp_nb.T.astype(np.float64) * points[:, None]) / (1.0 + d[:, None])  # (N, k)
    value = (weight * conv).sum(axis=0) / 15.0        # (k,)
    return value

What matters is the *near miss that can still convert*: an opponent cell needing exactly one extra supporter, where an empty cell next to it is already supported by my territory (so the follow-through claim exists). Grading by deficit and multiplying by convertibility should pick candidates whose pressure actually converts, which f006 (cells flipping now) and f071 (flat near-miss credit) both miss.

    cand_empty_adj = adjacency[np.ix_(moves, np.arange(N))] & empty[None, :]  # (k, N)
    d1 = cand_empty_adj.astype(np.float64)

    # distance-2 empty cells: empty cells adjacent to some d=1 cell, excluding candidates and d=1 cells
    # reach2[j] for candidate i = any d1 cell adjacent to j
    reach2 = (d1 @ adjacency.astype(np.float64)) > 0  # (k, N)
    reach2 = reach2 & empty[None, :]
    # exclude candidates themselves
    reach2[np.arange(moves.shape[0]), moves] = False
    # exclude d=1 cells
    reach2 = reach2 & (~cand_empty_adj)

    d1f = d1
    d2f = reach2.astype(np.float64)

    weight = pts / (1.0 + oppcount)  # (N,)
    contrib = d1f * (weight / 1.0)[None, :] + d2f * (weight / 2.0)[None, :]
    values = contrib.sum(axis=1) / 30.0
    return values

A reach density that counts d=1 as well as d=2 cells and discounts exactly by the target's contestedness (instead of f059's hard no-opponent-neighbour cut) gives a graded, distance-normalised claim on the web race that the flat two-step sums cannot express.

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Tempo-weighted net flip ledger: (1-f)*G - f*B, f = remaining/(N-2), G = points I flip now /15, B = opponent's best one-ply flip-back value /15."""
    N = owner.shape[0]
    rem = max(0, (N - 2) - turn)
    f = rem / max(1, N - 2)

    moves = np.asarray(moves)
    k = moves.shape[0]
    pts = points.astype(np.float64)
    adj = adjacency

    # Neighbour counts before claim
    mine = (owner == 1)
    opp = (owner == -1)
    A1 = adj[:, mine].sum(axis=1).astype(np.float64)   # my neighbours per cell
    Ao = adj[:, opp].sum(axis=1).astype(np.float64)    # opp neighbours per cell

    opp_home = homes[1]

    # G: points of opponent non-home cells flipped by claiming each move
    G = np.zeros(k)
    # B: opponent's best one-ply grab value after my claim + flips
    B = np.zeros(k)

    for idx in range(k):
        c = moves[idx]
        # After claim: c becomes mine
        A1_after = A1.copy()
        Ao_after = Ao.copy()
        # c's neighbours: for each neighbour j of c, my count increases by 1
        nbrs_c = adj[c]
        A1_after[nbrs_c] += 1.0
        # c itself is now mine; its own counts don't matter for flip test of others
        # Determine flips: opponent cells adjacent to c, non-home, with A1_after[j] >= Ao_after[j]
        flip_mask = nbrs_c & opp & (np.arange(N) != opp_home) & (A1_after >= Ao_after)
        G[idx] = pts[flip_mask].sum()

        # Apply flips: flipped cells become mine
        flipped = flip_mask
        # Update ownership after claim + flips
        owner_after = owner.copy()
        owner_after[c] = 1
        owner_after[flipped] = 1

        # Recompute neighbour counts after claim+flips
        mine_after = (owner_after == 1)
        opp_after = (owner_after == -1)
        A1_new = adj[:, mine_after].sum(axis=1).astype(np.float64)
        Ao_new = adj[:, opp_after].sum(axis=1).astype(np.float64)

        # Empty cells adjacent to one of my cells after claim
        empty = (owner_after == 0)
        my_cells = np.where(mine_after)[0]
        adj_to_mine = adj[:, my_cells].any(axis=1) if my_cells.size > 0 else np.zeros(N, dtype=bool)
        candidates_e = empty & adj_to_mine

        if not candidates_e.any():
            B[idx] = 0.0
            continue

        # For each such empty cell e, opponent claims it: e becomes opp
        # Then flips: my non-home cells adjacent to e with Ao_new[j]+1 >= A1_new[j]
        e_idx = np.where(candidates_e)[0]
        my_home = homes[0]
        best = 0.0
        for e in e_idx:
            nbrs_e = adj[e]
            # after opp claims e, opp count for neighbours of e increases by 1
            Ao_e = Ao_new.copy()
            Ao_e[nbrs_e] += 1.0
            flip_mask_e = nbrs_e & mine_after & (np.arange(N) != my_home) & (Ao_e >= A1_new)
            val = pts[flip_mask_e].sum()
            if val > best:
                best = val
        B[idx] = best

    G = G / 15.0
    B = B / 15.0
    return (1.0 - f) * G - f * B

idea.hypothesis: A flip's worth depends on how many claims remain to undo it: early flips are transient while the opponent's reply is imminent, late flips are final. All tried net-flip features are static, so they cannot express this. Writing G (points I flip now) with weight (elapsed/(N-2)) and B (the opponent's best one-ply flip-back value after my claim) with weight (remaining/(N-2)) makes the trade-off shift over the game, which the fixed-weight span of f006 and f031 cannot reproduce. If tempo is the missing ingredient, hex's lost_per_game (2.04) should fall.

G[k] = (1/15)*sum of points of opponent non-home cells that claiming move k flips (after the claim: A1[j]+1 >= Ao[j], j adjacent to move k, j != homes[1]). B[k] = (1/15)* the opponent's best one-ply grab value after my claim and its flips (same quantity as f031, negated sign removed): max over empty cells e adjacent to one of my cells after the claim of the points of my non-home cells e could flip. Return (1-f)*G - f*B, shape (k,).

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Uncontested two-step reach value E (f059) divided by (1 + flip gain G), per candidate."""
    N = owner.shape[0]
    empty = (owner == 0)
    opp = (owner == -1)
    my = (owner == 1)
    opp_home = homes[1]

    # opponent-neighbour mask per cell
    opp_nbr = (adjacency & opp[None, :]).any(axis=1)

    # empty adjacency among empty cells: empty_adj[i,j] = i~j and j empty
    empty_adj = (adjacency & empty[None, :]).astype(np.int32)

    # step-1 cells: empty neighbours of each candidate
    step1 = adjacency[moves] & empty[None, :]  # (k, N) bool

    # step-2 cells: empty cells adjacent to a step-1 cell
    step2 = (step1.astype(np.int32) @ empty_adj) > 0  # (k, N)

    # exclude candidate itself and its empty neighbours (step1)
    cand_mask = np.zeros((moves.shape[0], N), dtype=bool)
    cand_mask[np.arange(moves.shape[0]), moves] = True
    step2 = step2 & ~step1 & ~cand_mask

    # uncontested: no opponent neighbour
    uncontested = ~opp_nbr
    step2_unc = step2 & uncontested[None, :]

    E = (step2_unc.astype(np.float64) @ points.astype(np.float64)) / 30.0  # (k,)

    # flip gain G: opponent non-home cells adjacent to candidate that would flip
    my_nbr_count = (adjacency & my[None, :]).sum(axis=1)   # (N,)
    opp_nbr_count = (adjacency & opp[None, :]).sum(axis=1) # (N,)

    cand_adj_opp = adjacency[moves] & opp[None, :]  # (k, N)
    my_after = my_nbr_count[None, :] + cand_adj_opp.astype(np.int32)
    flips = cand_adj_opp & (my_after >= opp_nbr_count[None, :])
    flips[:, opp_home] = False

    G = (flips.astype(np.float64) @ points.astype(np.float64)) / 15.0  # (k,)

    return E / (1.0 + G)

idea.hypothesis: f059's uncontested two-step value is useful but blind to whether the same claim is also a flipping move. On flip-poor boards the reach is the whole story and should not be diluted by flip-heavy alternatives; the ratio E/(1+G) rewards reach on claims where nothing flips (the web/low-flip regime) and gives it up where a flip is available. If flip paucity is what makes reach decisive, this interaction should raise the value of the cells we actually claim on web.
idea.feature: E[k] = (1/30)*sum of points of empty cells reachable in exactly two claims from move k through empty cells, excluding move k and its empty neighbours, that have no opponent neighbour (the f059 quantity). G[k] = (1/15)*sum of points of opponent non-home cells flipped by claiming move k. Value = E / (1 + G), shape (k,).
idea.lesson: f078 (five point access, low-flip gated) and f086 (decision-level gate on f059) failed because the gate did not depend on the candidate; here the damping term G is per-candidate.

system:
You are the **Navigator** in Helix, an evolutionary search. You don't write candidates. You keep the search oriented: you maintain a map of **approaches** (the different ways the incumbent could be improved) and decide where the effort goes next.

Two loops do the work. The **deep loop** (a Researcher, then Coders) runs experiments on the approaches you assign. The **wide loop** (a Mutator) makes undirected variations of whatever you hand it, and of nothing else: it never sees approaches or hypotheses, only artefacts and scores.

## The approach tree

Each approach has a state:
- `untried`: brainstormed, not tested yet;
- `promising`: something under it gained on validation. Gets the most effort, and is split into deeper sub-approaches;
- `unproven`: tried without a gain, but nothing shows it can't work. Retried occasionally, at lower priority. Bad scores are not proof;
- `pruned`: the engine verified a certificate that everything under it adds nothing. Never assigned again.

## Each generation, decide

1. **Brainstorm** new approaches when the map is thin or the promising ones are drying up. Make them genuinely different from each other, and add deeper sub-approaches under promising ones.
2. **Assign the Researcher** to approaches, each with a mode: `explore` (an untried approach), `exploit` (deepen a promising one), `probe` (a cheap experiment to learn whether an unproven one has anything).
3. **Hand the Mutator parents**: ids from the ledger to vary. The engine already gives two slots to the most important kept features (variants of kept features win far more often); you choose the rest. Spread those: width means variety across approaches. Near-misses and surprising scores are good parents.
4. **Combinations**: pairs of features that each gained on their own but weren't kept, to retry together (some things only help next to another). A pair with a member that showed no gain alone is skipped: in testing, such pairs never gained.
5. **Prune requests**: approaches you believe are dead. The Prover will try to certify it; only a verified certificate prunes.

Effort follows evidence, but keep a share for the unproven and the untried: a search that only exploits stops finding things.

## Reply format

Start with the JSON block, then at most 80 words on your reasoning.

```json
{"new_approaches": [{"title": "<short>", "description": "<one sentence>", "parent": "<approach id or empty>"}],
 "research": [{"approach": "<id, or the exact title of a new approach>", "mode": "explore | exploit | probe", "why": "<one line>"}],
 "mutate": {"vary": ["<id>", "..."], "fresh": <how many fresh slots>},
 "combine": [["<id>", "<id>"]],
 "prune": ["<approach id>"]}
```

## What a candidate is here: a feature

The incumbent is a policy, a weighted sum of features; approaches are kinds of measurements (what quantity, under which conditions). Mutator parents are feature ids.

# The problem: Duel: play an invented territory game against a pool of scripted opponents

Play an invented two-player board game, "spore", against a fixed pool of scripted opponents. The policy is one player; it chooses its move each turn.

**The board.** A connected graph of about 30 cells. Each cell is worth 1, 2 or 5 points (about 60% are worth 1, 25% worth 2, 15% worth 5). Each player starts owning one *home* cell (worth 1); the two homes are far apart. All other cells start empty.

**A turn.** Players alternate. On your turn you must *claim* one empty cell that is adjacent to at least one cell you own; it becomes yours. Then *flips*: every opponent cell adjacent to the cell you just claimed (except the opponent's home, which never flips) becomes yours if, counting after your claim, you own at least as many of its neighbours as its owner does. Flips are decided all at once from the board right after the claim and do not chain: a flipped cell does not trigger further flips. A player with no legal claim (no empty cell next to its cells) passes and the other player continues.

**The end.** The game ends when no empty cell is left (about 30 claims in all, roughly half of them yours). Each player scores the points of the cells it owns at the end.

**One decision** = choosing which cell to claim. The **candidates** are your legal claims, in a random order (cells are also numbered at random). When there is only one legal claim it is taken automatically.

**Instances and cost.** An instance is 24 games on freshly generated boards of one family: 6 against each of the 4 opponents in the pool, moving first in half of them. The opponents are scripted players with different, fixed behaviour; their logic and identity are hidden, and you never see their future moves. The instance's **cost** is 100 x the opponents' share of all points scored in its games (in [0, 100]; the board's points are always all claimed). The **gap** is 100 x cost / the cost of Code Zero (the policy that always takes the first candidate, i.e. a random legal claim) on the same instance: Code Zero scores 100, lower is better. An opponent always keeps at least its home, so 0 is impossible; there is no known best.

Three training families, differing in board shape: `grid` (a 6 x 6 square grid, 4 random cells removed, 4 neighbours per cell), `hex` (a 6 x 5 hexagonal grid, 2 cells removed, up to 6 neighbours) and `web` (32 random points, each joined to its 3 nearest). The test split adds a board shape that training never shows.

## A feature

```python
import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """One line: exactly what this measures."""
    ...
    return values   # one number per candidate
```

- `moves`: shape (k,), int: the cells you may claim (the candidates), in random order. Index into the per-cell arrays below.
- `owner`: shape (N,), int8: for every cell on the board: 1 = yours, -1 = the opponent's, 0 = empty (N = number of cells).
- `homes`: shape (2,), int: your home cell and the opponent's home cell (homes never flip).
- `points`: shape (N,), int: what each cell is worth (1, 2 or 5).
- `adjacency`: shape (N, N), bool: which cells are neighbours (symmetric, False on the diagonal).
- `turn`: int: how many claims (by both players) have been made so far in this game; the game lasts N - 2 claims.
- Your current score is `points[owner == 1].sum()`, the opponent's `points[owner == -1].sum()`.
- Return one finite number per candidate (shape (k,)), or a few columns (shape (k, c)). The highest-scoring candidate is claimed.
- Import only `numpy` and `math`. No state between calls, no randomness, don't modify the inputs, no Python loops over candidates when a vectorised form exists (features run thousands of times per evaluation). Guard every division and log.
- Return finite numbers, roughly in [-1, 1] (normalise; the optimiser rescales anyway).

## How the policy works

priority(candidate) = w1 * feature1 + w2 * feature2 + ...; the highest priority wins; on a tie, the first candidate wins. With no features every candidate scores 0, so the first candidate always wins: that is **Code Zero**, the starting point (0% progress). An optimiser fits the weights, including their signs. A new feature is kept only if the policy does better with it than the same refit without it, on training instances *and* on separate validation instances, and the gain isn't already given by the kept features.

## How policies are scored

Per instance, the **gap** is how far the solution is above a reference (lower is better). The score is the mean gap over families. **Progress** is the share of the way from Code Zero (0%) to the best reachable (100%).

# The problem: Duel: play an invented territory game against a pool of scripted opponents

Play an invented two-player board game, "spore", against a fixed pool of scripted opponents. The policy is one player; it chooses its move each turn.

**The board.** A connected graph of about 30 cells. Each cell is worth 1, 2 or 5 points (about 60% are worth 1, 25% worth 2, 15% worth 5). Each player starts owning one *home* cell (worth 1); the two homes are far apart. All other cells start empty.

**A turn.** Players alternate. On your turn you must *claim* one empty cell that is adjacent to at least one cell you own; it becomes yours. Then *flips*: every opponent cell adjacent to the cell you just claimed (except the opponent's home, which never flips) becomes yours if, counting after your claim, you own at least as many of its neighbours as its owner does. Flips are decided all at once from the board right after the claim and do not chain: a flipped cell does not trigger further flips. A player with no legal claim (no empty cell next to its cells) passes and the other player continues.

**The end.** The game ends when no empty cell is left (about 30 claims in all, roughly half of them yours). Each player scores the points of the cells it owns at the end.

**One decision** = choosing which cell to claim. The **candidates** are your legal claims, in a random order (cells are also numbered at random). When there is only one legal claim it is taken automatically.

**Instances and cost.** An instance is 24 games on freshly generated boards of one family: 6 against each of the 4 opponents in the pool, moving first in half of them. The opponents are scripted players with different, fixed behaviour; their logic and identity are hidden, and you never see their future moves. The instance's **cost** is 100 x the opponents' share of all points scored in its games (in [0, 100]; the board's points are always all claimed). The **gap** is 100 x cost / the cost of Code Zero (the policy that always takes the first candidate, i.e. a random legal claim) on the same instance: Code Zero scores 100, lower is better. An opponent always keeps at least its home, so 0 is impossible; there is no known best.

Three training families, differing in board shape: `grid` (a 6 x 6 square grid, 4 random cells removed, 4 neighbours per cell), `hex` (a 6 x 5 hexagonal grid, 2 cells removed, up to 6 neighbours) and `web` (32 random points, each joined to its 3 nearest). The test split adds a board shape that training never shows.

# The problem: Duel: play an invented territory game against a pool of scripted opponents

Play an invented two-player board game, "spore", against a fixed pool of scripted opponents. The policy is one player; it chooses its move each turn.

**The board.** A connected graph of about 30 cells. Each cell is worth 1, 2 or 5 points (about 60% are worth 1, 25% worth 2, 15% worth 5). Each player starts owning one *home* cell (worth 1); the two homes are far apart. All other cells start empty.

**A turn.** Players alternate. On your turn you must *claim* one empty cell that is adjacent to at least one cell you own; it becomes yours. Then *flips*: every opponent cell adjacent to the cell you just claimed (except the opponent's home, which never flips) becomes yours if, counting after your claim, you own at least as many of its neighbours as its owner does. Flips are decided all at once from the board right after the claim and do not chain: a flipped cell does not trigger further flips. A player with no legal claim (no empty cell next to its cells) passes and the other player continues.

**The end.** The game ends when no empty cell is left (about 30 claims in all, roughly half of them yours). Each player scores the points of the cells it owns at the end.

**One decision** = choosing which cell to claim. The **candidates** are your legal claims, in a random order (cells are also numbered at random). When there is only one legal claim it is taken automatically.

**Instances and cost.** An instance is 24 games on freshly generated boards of one family: 6 against each of the 4 opponents in the pool, moving first in half of them. The opponents are scripted players with different, fixed behaviour; their logic and identity are hidden, and you never see their future moves. The instance's **cost** is 100 x the opponents' share of all points scored in its games (in [0, 100]; the board's points are always all claimed). The **gap** is 100 x cost / the cost of Code Zero (the policy that always takes the first candidate, i.e. a random legal claim) on the same instance: Code Zero scores 100, lower is better. An opponent always keeps at least its home, so 0 is impossible; there is no known best.

Play an invented two-player board game, "spore", against a fixed pool of scripted opponents. The policy is one player; it chooses its move each turn.

**The board.** A connected graph of about 30 cells. Each cell is worth 1, 2 or 5 points (about 60% are worth 1, 25% worth 2, 15% worth 5). Each player starts owning one *home* cell (worth 1); the two homes are far apart. All other cells start empty.

**A turn.** Players alternate. On your turn you must *claim* one empty cell that is adjacent to at least one cell you own; it becomes yours. Then *flips*: every opponent cell adjacent to the cell you just claimed (except the opponent's home, which never flips) becomes yours if, counting after your claim, you own at least as many of its neighbours as its owner does. Flips are decided all at once from the board right after the claim and do not chain: a flipped cell does not trigger further flips. A player with no legal claim (no empty cell next to its cells) passes and the other player continues.

**The end.** The game ends when no empty cell is left (about 30 claims in all, roughly half of them yours). Each player scores the points of the cells it owns at the end.

**One decision** = choosing which cell to claim. The **candidates** are your legal claims, in a random order (cells are also numbered at random). When there is only one legal claim it is taken automatically.

**Instances and cost.** An instance is 24 games on freshly generated boards of one family: 6 against each of the 4 opponents in the pool, moving first in half of them. The opponents are scripted players with different, fixed behaviour; their logic and identity are hidden, and you never see their future moves. The instance's **cost** is 100 x the opponents' share of all points scored in its games (in [0, 100]; the board's points are always all claimed). The **gap** is 100 x cost / the cost of Code Zero (the policy that always takes the first candidate, i.e. a random legal claim) on the same instance: Code Zero scores 100, lower is better. An opponent always keeps at least its home, so 0 is impossible; there is no known best.

Three training families, differing in board shape: `grid` (a 6 x 6 square grid, 4 random cells removed, 4 neighbours per cell), `hex` (a 6 x 5 hexagonal grid, 2 cells removed, up to 6 neighbours) and `web` (32 random points, each joined to its 3 nearest). The test split adds a board shape that training never shows.

- `owner`: shape (N,), int8: for every cell on the board: 1 = yours, -1 = the opponent's, 0 = empty (N = number of cells).
- `homes`: shape (2,), int: your home cell and the opponent's home cell (homes never flip).
- `points`: shape (N,), int: what each cell is worth (1, 2 or 5).
- `adjacency`: shape (N, N), bool: which cells are neighbours (symmetric, False on the diagonal).
- `turn`: int: how many claims (by both players) have been made so far in this game; the game lasts N - 2 claims.
- Your current score is `points[owner == 1].sum()`, the opponent's `points[owner == -1].sum()`.
- Return one finite number per candidate (shape (k,)), or a few columns (shape (k, c)). The highest-scoring candidate is claimed.
- Import only `numpy` and `math`. No state between calls, no randomness, don't modify the inputs, no Python loops over candidates when a vectorised form exists (features run thousands of times per evaluation). Guard every division and log.
- Return finite numbers, roughly in [-1, 1] (normalise; the optimiser rescales anyway).

## How the policy works

priority(candidate) = w1 * feature1 + w2 * feature2 + ...; the highest priority wins; on a tie, the first candidate wins. With no features every candidate scores 0, so the first candidate always wins: that is **Code Zero**, the starting point (0% progress). An optimiser fits the weights, including their signs. A new feature is kept only if the policy does better with it than the same refit without it, on training instances *and* on separate validation instances, and the gain isn't already given by the kept features.

## How policies are scored

Per instance, the **gap** is how far the solution is above a reference (lower is better). The score is the mean gap over families. **Progress** is the share of the way from Code Zero (0%) to the best reachable (100%).

# The problem: Duel: play an invented territory game against a pool of scripted opponents

Play an invented two-player board game, "spore", against a fixed pool of scripted opponents. The policy is one player; it chooses its move each turn.

**The board.** A connected graph of about 30 cells. Each cell is worth 1, 2 or 5 points (about 60% are worth 1, 25% worth 2, 15% worth 5). Each player starts owning one *home* cell (worth 1); the two homes are far apart. All other cells start empty.

**A turn.** Players alternate. On your turn you must *claim* one empty cell that is adjacent to at least one cell you own; it becomes yours. Flips are decided all at once from the board right after the claim and do not chain: a flipped cell does not trigger further flips. A player with no legal claim (no empty cell next to its cells) passes and the other player continues.

**The end.** The game ends when no empty cell is left (about 30 claims in all, roughly half of them yours). Each player scores the points of the cells it owns at the end.

**One decision** = choosing which cell to claim. The **candidates** are your legal claims, in a random order (cells are also numbered at random). When there is only one legal claim it is taken automatically.

**Instances and cost.** An instance is 24 games on freshly generated boards of one family: 6 against each of the 4 opponents in the pool, moving first in half of them. The opponents are scripted players with different, fixed behaviour; their logic and identity are hidden, and you never see their future moves. The instance's **cost** is 100 x the opponents' share of all points scored in its games (in [0, 100]; the board's points are always all claimed). The **gap** is 100 x cost / the cost of Code Zero (the policy that always takes the first candidate, i.e. a random legal claim) on the same instance: Code Zero scores 100, lower is better. An opponent always keeps at least its home, so 0 is impossible; there is no known best.

```python
    out = np.zeros(moves.shape[0], dtype=np.float64)
    for i, c in enumerate(moves):
        adj_c = adjacency[c]
        # flips from claiming c
        flips = adj_c & opp & not_home_mask & (A1f + 1.0 >= Aof)
        # after my claim: mine2, opp2
        mine2 = mine | flips
        mine2[c] = True
        opp2 = opp & ~flips
        # recompute vulnerability
        A1b = adjacency @ mine2.astype(np.int64)
        Aob = adjacency @ opp2.astype(np.int64)
        vuln2 = mine2 & (np.arange(N) != my_home) & (Aob + 1 >= A1b)
        vuln2_pts = np.where(vuln2, pts, 0.0)
        opp_legal2 = empty & ~np.eye(N, dtype=bool)[c] & ((adjacency @ opp2.astype(np.int64)) > 0)
        # opp_legal2: empty, not c, adjacent to opp2
        retal2 = adjacency @ vuln2_pts
        retal2 = np.where(opp_legal2, retal2, 0.0)
        worst = retal2.max() if retal2.size else 0.0
        out[i] = -worst / 5.0
    return out
```

You are the **Researcher** in Helix, an evolutionary search. You are the deep loop: you work out *why* the current best candidate loses where it does, and you design experiments that find out. The Mutator, another agent, makes undirected variations; you cash in on what it stumbles on and on what your own experiments reveal.

## What you get

- the incumbent (the current best) and its parts: what each part actually does and how much the result relies on it;
- **diagnostics**: named metrics of the incumbent's results, next to a reference where one exists. This is where the mechanism shows;
- **sensitivity probes**: each part of the incumbent knocked out, weakened and amplified. A gain from amplifying means a direction is under-used; a loss from weakening means the incumbent relies on it;
- the **ledger** for the approaches you're assigned: what was tried, how it scored, and whether its prediction held;
- the **Mutator's recent finds**: things that scored well or nearly well without anyone knowing why. Explaining and sharpening a lucky find is often the best experiment available;
- your **assignments** from the Navigator: which approaches to work on, and how (explore a new one, exploit a promising one, probe a doubtful one).

## How to work

1. **Find a mechanism, not a symptom.** Name a concrete difference between the incumbent's results and the reference (or between what works and what doesn't), and the decision that produces it.
2. **Design experiments of two kinds:**
   - `probe`: written to *learn*. Change one thing, or exaggerate one aspect, so the result tells you whether that aspect matters. Judged by whether its prediction held, not by its score.
   - `improve`: written to *win*.
3. **Don't repeat the ledger.** If an idea was tried, change it meaningfully or leave it. A disguised copy is detected and discarded. When the ledger shows a group of tried features that behave alike, that idea is spent: look at a different quantity altogether.
4. **Learn from what failed.** A prediction that didn't hold means the mechanism you believed is wrong or incomplete. Say what it taught you (`lesson`) before proposing the next experiment.
5. **Predict.** Every experiment names one metric from the diagnostics, where it should move (a family or scope), and the direction. The engine checks it.
6. **Be exact** in `change`: describe the candidate so precisely that it can be written without guessing.

Start with the JSON block, then at most 120 words on what you think is going on.

## What a candidate is here: a feature

The incumbent is a policy: a weighted sum of **features** (measurements of a candidate in one decision). An optimiser fits the weights and their signs, so never choose numbers or signs: choose *what to measure*. The parts in the sensitivity probes are the kept features; amplifying one means multiplying its weight.

- `change` is the exact measurement, per candidate, in terms of the arguments, so a Coder can write it without guessing. Say what it is for the last or special candidates when that matters.
- **It must rank candidates differently.** A value that is the same for every candidate in a decision, or a monotone copy of a feature the policy already has, tells the optimiser nothing. Prefer comparisons between normalised quantities; use a hard threshold only when the condition is the idea.
- A `probe` feature changes one thing, or exaggerates one aspect (a sharper threshold, a stronger form, one condition only).

A feature may apply only under a condition (only in some decisions, or for some candidates, when a quantity crosses a threshold) and be zero otherwise. The policy is one weighted sum, so a condition is the only way it can treat different cases differently.

# The problem: Duel: play an invented territory game against a pool of scripted opponents

Play an invented two-player board game, "spore", against a fixed pool of scripted opponents. The policy is one player; it chooses its move each turn.

**The board.** A connected graph of about 30 cells. Each cell is worth 1, 2 or 5 points (about 60% are worth 1, 25% worth 2, 15% worth 5). Each player starts owning one *home* cell (worth 1); the two homes are far apart. All other cells start empty.

**A turn.** Players alternate. On your turn you must *claim* one empty cell that is adjacent to at least one cell you own; it becomes yours. Then *flips*: every opponent cell adjacent to the cell you just claimed (except the opponent's home, which never flips) becomes yours if, counting after your claim, you own at least as many of its neighbours as its owner does. Flips are decided all at once from the board right after the claim and do not chain: a flipped cell does not trigger further flips. A player with no legal claim (no empty cell next to its cells) passes and the other player continues.

**The end.** The game ends when no empty cell is left (about 30 claims in all, roughly half of them yours). Each player scores the points of the cells it owns at the end.

**One decision** = choosing which cell to claim. The **candidates** are your legal claims, in a random order (cells are also numbered at random). When there is only one legal claim it is taken automatically.

**Instances and cost.** An instance is 24 games on freshly generated boards of one family: 6 against each of the 4 opponents in the pool, moving first in half of them. The opponents are scripted players with different, fixed behaviour; their logic and identity are hidden, and you never see their future moves. The instance's **cost** is 100 x the opponents' share of all points scored in its games (in [0, 100]; the board's points are always all claimed). The **gap** is 100 x cost / the cost of Code Zero (the policy that always takes the first candidate, i.e. a random legal claim) on the same instance: Code Zero scores 100, lower is better. An opponent always keeps at least its home, so 0 is impossible; there is no known best.

Three training families, differing in board shape: `grid` (a 6 x 6 square grid, 4 random cells removed, 4 neighbours per cell), `hex` (a 6 x 5 hexagonal grid, 2 cells removed, up to 6 neighbours) and `web` (32 random points, each joined to its 3 nearest). The test split adds a board shape that training never shows.

## How the policy works

priority(candidate) = w1 * feature1 + w2 * feature2 + ...; the highest priority wins; on a tie, the first candidate wins. With no features every candidate scores 0, so the first candidate always wins: that is **Code Zero**, the starting point (0% progress). An optimiser fits the weights, including their signs. A new feature is kept only if the policy does better with it than the same refit without it, on training instances *and* on separate validation instances, and the gain isn't already given by the kept features.

## How policies are scored

Per instance, the **gap** is how far the solution is above a reference (lower is better). The score is the mean gap over families. **Progress** is the share of the way from Code Zero (0%) to the best reachable (100%).

# The problem: Duel: play an invented territory game against a pool of scripted opponents

Play an invented two-player board game, "spore", against a fixed pool of scripted opponents. The policy is one player; it chooses its move each turn.

**The board.** A connected graph of about 30 cells. Each cell is worth 1, 2 or 5 points (about 60% are worth 1, 25% worth 2, 15% worth 5). Each player starts owning one *home* cell (worth 1); the two homes are far apart. All other cells start empty.

**A turn.** Players alternate. On your turn you must *claim* one empty cell that is adjacent to at least one cell you own; it becomes yours. Then *flips*: every opponent cell adjacent to the cell you just claimed (except the opponent's home, which never flips) becomes yours if, counting after your claim, you own at least as many of its neighbours as its owner does. Flips are decided all at once from the board right after the claim and do not chain: a flipped cell does not trigger further flips. A player with no legal claim (no empty cell next to its cells) passes and the other player continues.

**The end.** The game ends when no empty cell is left (about 30 claims in all, roughly half of them yours). Each player scores the points of the cells it owns at the end.

**One decision** = choosing which cell to claim. The **candidates** are your legal claims, in a random order (cells are also numbered at random). When there is only one legal claim it is taken automatically.

**Instances and cost.** An instance is 24 games on freshly generated boards of one family: 6 against each of the 4 opponents in the pool, moving first in half of them. The opponents are scripted players with different, fixed behaviour; their logic and identity are hidden, and you never see their future moves. The instance's **cost** is 100 x the opponents' share of all points scored in its games (in [0, 100]; the board's points are always all claimed). The **gap** is 100 x cost / the cost of Code Zero (the policy that always takes the first candidate, i.e. a random legal claim) on the same instance: Code Zero scores 100, lower is better. An opponent always keeps at least its home, so 0 is impossible; there is no known best.

Three training families, differing in board shape: `grid` (a 6 x 6 square grid, 4 random cells removed, 4 neighbours per cell), `hex` (a 6 x 5 hexagonal grid, 2 cells removed, up to 6 neighbours) and `web` (32 random points, each joined to its 3 nearest). The test split adds a board shape that training never shows.

```python
import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Sum of points of empty, opponent-unreachable cells at graph distance exactly 3 from each candidate, scaled by remaining-empty fraction and /30."""
    N = owner.shape[0]
    A = adjacency.astype(np.int32)
    D1 = A > 0
    D2 = (A @ A) > 0
    D3 = (D2.astype(np.int32) @ A) > 0
    M = D3 & ~D2 & ~D1  # shape (N, N): M[c, j] true iff dist(c, j) == 3

    opp = (owner == -1)
    opp_neighbour_count = A @ opp.astype(np.int32)  # per cell, number of opponent-owned neighbours
    safe = (owner == 0) & (opp_neighbour_count == 0)
    s = np.where(safe, points.astype(np.float64), 0.0)

    raw = M[moves].astype(np.float64) @ s  # shape (k,)
    value = raw / 30.0

    n_empty = int((owner == 0).sum())
    denom = max(N - 2, 1)
    decay = n_empty / denom
    return value * decay
```

This computes, for each candidate, the total points of empty cells at graph distance exactly 3 that have no opponent-owned neighbour, divided by 30 and multiplied by the fraction of cells still empty (empty count / (N-2)); I read "no opponent-owned neighbour" as zero opponent-owned adjacent cells and applied the decay factor uniformly to all entries.

```python
import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Two-step expansion value (points of empty cells at graph distance exactly 2 from c, /30) discounted by the fraction of c's empty neighbours that touch opponent territory."""
    moves = np.asarray(moves)
    owner = np.asarray(owner)
    points = np.asarray(points)
    adjacency = np.asarray(adjacency)

    empty = (owner == 0)
    opp = (owner == -1)

    # neighbours of each candidate
    cand_adj = adjacency[moves]  # (k, N)
    empty_neigh = cand_adj & empty[None, :]  # (k, N)

    # cells at graph distance exactly 2 from c: neighbours of empty neighbours, excluding c and c's neighbours
    # dist2 mask: (adjacency @ empty_neigh.T) > 0  -> (N, k)
    reach1 = empty_neigh.T.astype(np.int32)  # (N, k)
    dist2 = (adjacency.astype(np.int32) @ reach1) > 0  # (N, k)
    # exclude c itself and c's direct neighbours
    dist2 &= ~cand_adj.T  # (N, k)
    dist2 &= empty[:, None]  # only empty cells count

    E2 = (dist2 * points[:, None]).sum(axis=0)  # (k,)

    # exposure: empty neighbours of c that have at least one opponent neighbour
    opp_neigh = adjacency & opp[None, :]  # (N, N): cells adjacent to opponent
    has_opp_neigh = opp_neigh.any(axis=1)  # (N,)
    n_empty_neigh = empty_neigh.sum(axis=1)  # (k,)
    n_exposed = (empty_neigh & has_opp_neigh[None, :]).sum(axis=1)  # (k,)

    exposure = n_exposed / np.maximum(1, n_empty_neigh)

    value = (E2 / 30.0) * (1.0 - exposure)
    return value
```

This computes, per candidate, the sum of points of empty cells at graph distance exactly 2 (excluding the candidate and its direct neighbours) divided by 30, multiplied by one minus the fraction of the candidate's empty neighbours that are adjacent to at least one opponent-owned cell; I read "graph distance exactly 2" as reachable via one empty neighbour and not directly adjacent, and used `max(1, n_empty_neigh)` to guard the division.

```python
import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """(gross points flipped by the claim minus points of flipped cells the opponent can recapture next turn) / 15."""
    N = owner.shape[0]
    k = moves.shape[0]
    mine = (owner == 1)
    opp = (owner == -1)
    empty = (owner == 0)
    opp_home = homes[1]

    A1 = adjacency @ mine.astype(np.int64)   # my neighbour counts
    Ao = adjacency @ opp.astype(np.int64)    # opponent neighbour counts
    E = adjacency @ empty.astype(np.int64)   # empty neighbour counts

    adj_m = adjacency[moves]                 # (k, N)
    pts = points.astype(np.float64)

    # flipped[c,j]: opponent cell j (not opp home) adjacent to c, flips after my claim
    is_opp = opp[None, :] & (np.arange(N)[None, :] != opp_home)
    flips = adj_m & is_opp & ((A1[None, :] + 1) >= Ao[None, :])   # (k, N)

    # after claim: my count of j = A1[j] + adj_m[c,j]; opp count = Ao[j] - flips[c,j]
    my_after = A1[None, :] + adj_m.astype(np.int64)
    opp_after = Ao[None, :] - flips.astype(np.int64)

    # empty neighbours of j excluding c: E[j] - adj_m[c,j] (c is empty before the claim)
    empty_other = E[None, :] - adj_m.astype(np.int64)

    # recapturable: flipped and opponent can reach a flip with one empty neighbour e != c
    recapturable = flips & (empty_other >= 1) & ((opp_after + 1) >= my_after)

    G = (flips * pts[None, :]).sum(axis=1)
    R = (recapturable * pts[None, :]).sum(axis=1)

    return (G - R) / 15.0
```

# The problem: Duel: play an invented territory game against a pool of scripted opponents

Play an invented two-player board game, "spore", against a fixed pool of scripted opponents. The policy is one player; it chooses its move each turn.

**The board.** A connected graph of about 30 cells. Each cell is worth 1, 2 or 5 points (about 60% are worth 1, 25% worth 2, 15% worth 5). Each player starts owning one *home* cell (worth 1); the two homes are far apart. All other cells start empty.

**A turn.** Players alternate. On your turn you must *claim* one empty cell that is adjacent to at least one cell you own; it becomes yours. Then *flips*: every opponent cell adjacent to the cell you just claimed (except the opponent's home, which never flips) becomes yours if, counting after your claim, you own at least as many of its neighbours as its owner does. Flips are decided all at once from the board right after the claim and do not chain: a flipped cell does not trigger further flips. A player with no legal claim (no empty cell next to its cells) passes and the other player continues.

**The end.** The game ends when no empty cell is left (about 30 claims in all, roughly half of them yours). Each player scores the points of the cells it owns at the end.

**One decision** = choosing which cell to claim. The **candidates** are your legal claims, in a random order (cells are also numbered at random). When there is only one legal claim it is taken automatically.

**Instances and cost.** An instance is 24 games on freshly generated boards of one family: 6 against each of the 4 opponents in the pool, moving first in half of them. The opponents are scripted players with different, fixed behaviour; their logic and identity are hidden, and you never see their future moves. The instance's **cost** is 100 x the opponents' share of all points scored in its games (in [0, 100]; the board's points are always all claimed). The **gap** is 100 x cost / the cost of Code Zero (the policy that always takes the first candidate, i.e. a random legal claim) on the same instance: Code Zero scores 100, lower is better. import numpy as np

```python
def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
```
```python
    """Endgame (<=8 empty cells) two-ply net swing: my claim points + my flips minus opponent's best grab-and-flip reply, /30."""
    k = moves.shape[0]

    my_home = homes[0]
    opp_home = homes[1]
    N = owner.shape[0]

    for idx in range(k):
        c = moves[idx]
        # post-claim board
        post = owner.copy()
        post[c] = 1
        # flips: opponent cells adjacent to c, not opp home, my neighbours >= opp neighbours
        G = 0
        for j in range(N):
            if post[j] == -1 and j != opp_home and adjacency[c, j]:
                my_n = int(((post == 1) & adjacency[j]).sum())
                opp_n = int(((post == -1) & adjacency[j]).sum())
                if my_n >= opp_n:
                    post[j] = 1
                    G += int(points[j])
        V = int(points[c])

        # opponent legal replies: empty cells adjacent to opponent territory in post board
        opp_terr = (post == -1)
        empty_mask = (post == 0)
        adj_to_opp = (adjacency & opp_terr[:, None]).any(axis=0)
        legal = empty_mask & adj_to_opp

        R = 0
        if legal.any():
            for e in np.nonzero(legal)[0]:
                # opponent claims e
                post2 = post.copy()
                post2[e] = -1
                # flips: my cells adjacent to e, not my home, opp neighbours >= my neighbours
                flip_pts = 0
                for j in range(N):
```

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Two-step expansion value (points of empty cells at graph distance exactly 2 from c, /30) discounted by the fraction of c's empty neighbours that touch opponent territory."""
    moves = np.asarray(moves)
    owner = np.asarray(owner)
    points = np.asarray(points)
    adjacency = np.asarray(adjacency)

    empty = (owner == 0)
    opp = (owner == -1)

    # neighbours of each candidate
    cand_adj = adjacency[moves]  # (k, N)
    empty_neigh = cand_adj & empty[None, :]  # (k, N)

    # cells at graph distance exactly 2 from c: neighbours of empty neighbours, excluding c and c's neighbours
    # dist2 mask: (adjacency @ empty_neigh.T) > 0  -> (N, k)
    reach1 = empty_neigh.T.astype(np.int32)  # (N, k)
    dist2 = (adjacency.astype(np.int32) @ reach1) > 0  # (N, k)
    # exclude c itself and c's direct neighbours
    dist2 &= ~cand_adj.T  # (N, k)
    dist2 &= empty[:, None]  # only empty cells count

    E2 = (dist2 * points[:, None]).sum(axis=0)  # (k,)

    # exposure: empty neighbours of c that have at least one opponent neighbour
    opp_neigh = adjacency & opp[None, :]  # (N, N): cells adjacent to opponent
    has_opp_neigh = opp_neigh.any(axis=1)  # (N,)
    n_empty_neigh = empty_neigh.sum(axis=1)  # (k,)
    n_exposed = (empty_neigh & has_opp_neigh[None, :]).sum(axis=1)  # (k,)

    exposure = n_exposed / np.maximum(1, n_empty_neigh)

    value = (E2 / 30.0) * (1.0 - exposure)
    return value

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """(gross points flipped by the claim minus points of flipped cells the opponent can recapture next turn) / 15."""
    N = owner.shape[0]
    k = moves.shape[0]
    mine = (owner == 1)
    opp = (owner == -1)
    empty = (owner == 0)
    opp_home = homes[1]

    A1 = adjacency @ mine.astype(np.int64)   # my neighbour counts
    Ao = adjacency @ opp.astype(np.int64)    # opponent neighbour counts
    E = adjacency @ empty.astype(np.int64)   # empty neighbour counts

    adj_m = adjacency[moves]                 # (k, N)
    pts = points.astype(np.float64)

    # flipped[c,j]: opponent cell j (not opp home) adjacent to c, flips after my claim
    is_opp = opp[None, :] & (np.arange(N)[None, :] != opp_home)
    flips = adj_m & is_opp & ((A1[None, :] + 1) >= Ao[None, :])   # (k, N)

    # after claim: my count of j = A1[j] + adj_m[c,j]; opp count = Ao[j] - flips[c,j]
    my_after = A1[None, :] + adj_m.astype(np.int64)
    opp_after = Ao[None, :] - flips.astype(np.int64)

    # empty neighbours of j excluding c: E[j] - adj_m[c,j] (c is empty before the claim)
    empty_other = E[None, :] - adj_m.astype(np.int64)

    # recapturable: flipped and opponent can reach a flip with one empty neighbour e != c
    recapturable = flips & (empty_other >= 1) & ((opp_after + 1) >= my_after)

    G = (flips * pts[None, :]).sum(axis=1)
    R = (recapturable * pts[None, :]).sum(axis=1)

    return (G - R) / 15.0

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Negative opponent follow-up swing: best (points grabbed + my points flipped back) over opponent claims after mine, minus my gain from the claim itself, /30, only counting opponent claims that would actually flip one of my cells."""
    N = owner.shape[0]
    my_home = int(homes[0])
    opp_home = int(homes[1])
    mine = (owner == 1)
    opp = (owner == -1)
    empty = (owner == 0)
    A1 = adjacency @ mine.astype(np.int64)
    Ao = adjacency @ opp.astype(np.int64)
    pts = points.astype(np.float64)
    idx_all = np.arange(N)
    not_my_home = idx_all != my_home
    not_opp_home = idx_all != opp_home
    Af = adjacency.astype(np.float64)

    out = np.zeros(moves.shape[0], dtype=np.float64)
    for idx in range(moves.shape[0]):
        c = moves[idx]
        adj_c = adjacency[c]
        flips = adj_c & opp & not_opp_home & ((A1 + 1) >= Ao)
        my_gain = pts[c] + pts[flips].sum()
        mine2 = mine.copy()
        mine2[c] = True
        mine2 |= flips
        opp2 = opp & ~flips
        A1b = adjacency @ mine2.astype(np.int64)
        Aob = adjacency @ opp2.astype(np.int64)
        legal_e = empty & (Aob > 0)
        if not legal_e.any():
            out[idx] = 0.0
            continue
        # cells of mine2 that opponent could flip back
        flip_back_mask = mine2 & not_my_home & ((Aob + 1) >= A1b)
        flip_back_pts = np.where(flip_back_mask, pts, 0.0)
        # opponent swing for claiming e: pts[e] + my flipped-back points adjacent to e
        gain = pts + Af @ flip_back_pts
        # only consider opponent claims that flip something of mine (aggressive grabs)
        flips_any = (Af @ flip_back_mask.astype(np.float64)) > 0
        aggressive = legal_e & flips_any
        if aggressive.any():
            best = gain[aggressive].max()
        else:
            best = 0.0
        out[idx] = -(best - my_gain) / 30.0
    return out
feature.measures: Negative opponent follow-up swing: best (points grabbed + my points flipped back) over opponent claims after mine, minus my gain from the claim itself, /30, only counting opponent claims that would actually flip one of my cells.

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """For each candidate: points of empty cells at distance 2 from it that the opponent cannot reach on its very next claim (no opponent-owned neighbour, not adjacent to c, not in the distance-1 shell), minus a penalty for distance-2 cells that ARE opponent-grabbable next turn — a signed safe/contested split, divided by 30."""
    E = (owner == 0)
    N = owner.shape[0]
    pts = points.astype(np.float64)
    opp = (owner == -1)
    # cells the opponent can claim next: empty with an opponent-owned neighbour
    opp_reach = E & ((adjacency @ opp.astype(np.int64)) > 0)
    mine = (owner == 1)
    my_reach = E & ((adjacency @ mine.astype(np.int64)) > 0)
    safe = E & ~opp_reach
    Af = adjacency.astype(np.float64)
    A = adjacency[moves]                       # (k, N)
    s1 = A & E[None, :]                        # empty neighbours of each candidate
    reach2 = ((s1.astype(np.float64) @ Af) > 0) & E[None, :] & ~s1 & ~A
    safe2 = reach2 & safe[None, :]
    # contested distance-2: cells that are opponent-reachable right now and that I can only reach in 2
    contested2 = reach2 & opp_reach[None, :] & ~my_reach[None, :]
    values = (safe2.astype(np.float64) @ pts - 0.5 * (contested2.astype(np.float64) @ pts)) / 30.0
    return values

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Negative, per candidate, of the points at risk if the opponent claims its best-flipping empty neighbour next turn: for every empty cell adjacent to the candidate, simulate the opponent claiming it, sum the points of my cells it would flip, take the best (worst for me), /15. Zero if no such threat exists."""
    N = owner.shape[0]
    my = (owner == 1)
    opp = (owner == -1)
    empty = (owner == 0)
    my_home = homes[0]
    pts = points.astype(np.float64)

    A1 = adjacency @ my.astype(np.int64)
    Ao = adjacency @ opp.astype(np.int64)

    adj_c = adjacency[moves]                      # (k, N) neighbours of each candidate
    threat_cells = adj_c & empty[None, :]         # (k, N) empty cells opponent could grab next to c
    # restrict to cells the opponent can actually claim (adjacent to some opp cell)
    reachable = (Ao > 0)
    threat_cells = threat_cells & reachable[None, :]

    # For each (candidate, threat cell e): which of MY cells would flip if opp claims e.
    # opp claims e: Ao[j] + 1 >= A1[j]  for my cell j adjacent to e, j != my home.
    not_home = np.ones(N, dtype=bool)
    not_home[my_home] = False
    flip_cond_my = ((Ao[None, :] + 1) >= A1[None, :]) & my[None, :] & not_home[None, :]  # (1,N) which my cells would flip given e adjacent
    # flip_pts_vec[j] = points[j] if my[j] and flips
    flip_pts_vec = np.where(flip_cond_my[0], pts, 0.0)   # (N,)

    # For each candidate c and each threat cell e adjacent to c: value = sum over my neighbours of e of flip_pts_vec
    # = (adjacency @ flip_pts_vec)[e] summed over e in threat_cells[c]
    cell_flip_value = adjacency.astype(np.float64) @ flip_pts_vec   # (N,) points lost if opp claims each cell
    cell_flip_value = cell_flip_value * (~ (np.arange(N) == my_home))

    # best threat per candidate: max over e in threat_cells[c] of cell_flip_value[e]
    masked = np.where(threat_cells, cell_flip_value[None, :], -1.0)
    best = masked.max(axis=1)
    best = np.where(best < 0.0, 0.0, best)
    return -best / 15.0
feature.measures: Negative, per candidate, of the points at risk if the opponent claims its best-flipping empty neighbour next turn: for every empty cell adjacent to the candidate, simulate the opponent claiming it, sum the points of my cells it would flip, take the best (worst for me), /15. Zero if no such threat exists.

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Negative of the points of the single highest-value empty cell that the opponent could claim next turn and that would flip one of my cells, divided by 5 — measures the worst immediate retaliation available to the opponent, only late in the game."""
    N = owner.shape[0]
    mine = (owner == 1)
    opp = (owner == -1)
    empty = (owner == 0)
    pts = points.astype(np.float64)
    my_home = homes[0]

    # My cells vulnerable to flipping: not my home, and opponent already has >= my count - 1 neighbours
    A1 = adjacency @ mine.astype(np.int64)
    Ao = adjacency @ opp.astype(np.int64)
    vulnerable = mine & (np.arange(N) != my_home) & (Ao + 1 >= A1)

    if not vulnerable.any():
        return np.zeros(moves.shape[0], dtype=np.float64)

    # For each empty cell e the opponent could claim (adjacent to opp territory),
    # which vulnerable cells would flip? A vulnerable cell j flips from e iff e is its neighbour
    # and after opp claims e: Ao[j]+1 >= A1[j] (already true by vulnerability).
    # Value of the retaliation = points of j (lost) captured via claiming e.
    # So value[e] = sum of points of vulnerable neighbours of e.
    vuln_pts = np.where(vulnerable, pts, 0.0)
    # opp-legal empties: empty cells adjacent to opponent territory
    opp_legal = empty & ((adjacency @ opp.astype(np.int64)) > 0)
    # retaliation value per empty cell
    retal = adjacency @ vuln_pts  # sum of vulnerable-neighbour points
    retal = np.where(opp_legal, retal, 0.0)

    # For each candidate: after my claim+flips, would reduce the opponent's opportunities.
    # Approximate: my claim removes one empty cell (the candidate) and flips some opp cells.
    # Score = -(worst retaliation remaining after my claim) / 5
    A1f = A1.astype(np.float64)
    Aof = Ao.astype(np.float64)
    not_home_mask = (np.arange(N) != homes[1])

    out = np.zeros(moves.shape[0], dtype=np.float64)
    for i, c in enumerate(moves):
        adj_c = adjacency[c]
        # flips from claiming c
        flips = adj_c & opp & not_home_mask & (A1f + 1.0 >= Aof)
        # after my claim: mine2, opp2
        mine2 = mine | flips
        mine2[c] = True
        opp2 = opp & ~flips
        # recompute vulnerability
        A1b = adjacency @ mine2.astype(np.int64)
        Aob = adjacency @ opp2.astype(np.int64)
        vuln2 = mine2 & (np.arange(N) != my_home) & (Aob + 1 >= A1b)
        vuln2_pts = np.where(vuln2, pts, 0.0)
        opp_legal2 = empty & ~np.eye(N, dtype=bool)[c] & ((adjacency @ opp2.astype(np.int64)) > 0)
        # opp_legal2: empty, not c, adjacent to opp2
        retal2 = adjacency @ vuln2_pts
        retal2 = np.where(opp_legal2, retal2, 0.0)
        worst = retal2.max() if retal2.size else 0.0
        out[i] = -worst / 5.0
    return out

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Negative BFS distance from each candidate to the opponent's home, but weighted by the point value of the cells on that path's frontier: candidates whose short path to the enemy home runs through low-value empty cells are favoured (denial), normalised by N."""
    N = adjacency.shape[0]
    target = int(homes[1])
    dist = np.full(N, -1, dtype=np.int64)
    dist[target] = 0
    frontier = np.array([target], dtype=np.int64)
    while frontier.size > 0:
        nb = adjacency[frontier].any(axis=0)
        nb[dist >= 0] = False
        nxt = np.nonzero(nb)[0]
        dist[nxt] = dist[frontier].min() + 1
        frontier = nxt
    d = dist[moves].astype(np.float64)
    d[d < 0] = N
    # value of empty cells adjacent to each candidate, that lie on a shortest path toward opp home
    dist_all = dist.astype(np.float64)
    dist_all[dist_all < 0] = N
    # candidate's own distance to target
    dm = dist_all[moves]  # (k,)
    # for each candidate, average value of its empty neighbours that are closer to the target
    closer = (dist_all[None, :] < dm[:, None]) & (owner == 0)[None, :]
    nb_mask = adjacency[moves] & closer

    return (-d / float(N)) * (0.5 + 0.5 * (1.0 - meanval / 5.0))

        gain = pts + adjacency @ flip_back_pts
        best = gain[legal_e].max()
        out[idx] = -best / 30.0
    return out

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Negative points of each candidate times the capped count of empty neighbours from which the opponent could claim and flip it next turn."""
    N = owner.shape[0]
    my = (owner == 1)
    opp = (owner == -1)
    empty = (owner == 0)
    opp_home = homes[1]

    A1 = adjacency @ my.astype(np.int64)      # my neighbours per cell
    Ao = adjacency @ opp.astype(np.int64)    # opponent neighbours per cell

    # opponent cells that would flip if I claim c (per candidate)
    # flips[j] = opp cell j adjacent to c, j != opp home, A1[j] + 1 >= Ao[j]
    adj_c = adjacency[moves]                 # (k, N)
    is_opp = opp[None, :]
    not_home = np.ones(N, dtype=bool)
    not_home[opp_home] = False
    flip_cond = (A1[None, :] + 1 >= Ao[None, :])
    flips = adj_c & is_opp & not_home[None, :] & flip_cond   # (k, N)

    f_nb = flips.astype(np.int64)            # (k, N) flipped neighbours of c

    n_my = A1[moves] + f_nb.sum(axis=1)      # (k,)
    n_opp = Ao[moves] - f_nb.sum(axis=1)     # (k,)

    # opp2 = opponent cells not flipped; Aob = their neighbour counts
    opp2 = opp[None, :] & ~flips             # (k, N)
    Aob = opp2.astype(np.int64) @ adjacency.astype(np.int64)  # (k, N)

    threat = empty[None, :] & adj_c & (Aob > 0) & (n_opp[:, None] + 1 >= n_my[:, None])

    tcount = np.minimum(threat.sum(axis=1), 2).astype(np.float64)
    value = -(points[moves].astype(np.float64) / 5.0) * (tcount / 2.0)
    return value

feature.code:
import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Sum over opponent cells adjacent to the candidate of points * (my-neighbour surplus toward flip), i.e. how close each adjacent opponent cell is to flipping, weighted by value, /15."""
    A1 = (adjacency & (owner == 1)[None, :]).sum(1).astype(np.float64)
    Ao = (adjacency & (owner == -1)[None, :]).sum(1).astype(np.float64)
    cand = adjacency[moves]
    opp_nb = cand & (owner == -1)[None, :]
    # margin: A1+1 - Ao  (>=0 means flips).  Use a soft proximity: 1/(1+max(margin,0)) so
    # already-flipping (margin>=0) cells count fully and near-miss cells (margin<0) count partially.
    margin = (A1[None, :] + 1.0) - Ao[None, :]
    prox = np.where(margin >= 0.0, 1.0, 1.0 / (1.0 + (-margin)))
    w = opp_nb.astype(np.float64) * prox * points[None, :].astype(np.float64)
    w[:, homes[1]] = 0.0
    return w.sum(1) / 15.0
feature.measures: Sum over opponent cells adjacent to the candidate of points * (my-neighbour surplus toward flip), i.e. how close each adjacent opponent cell is to flipping, weighted by value, /15.

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Two-step expansion value only counting cells the OPPONENT cannot reach first: for each candidate, sum of points of empty cells at graph distance exactly 2 (excluding c and distance-1 shells) that are NOT adjacent to any opponent-owned cell, divided by 30. Zero late in the game once few empty cells remain."""

    N = owner.shape[0]
    pts = points.astype(np.float64)
    opp = (owner == -1)
    # cells adjacent to opponent territory (contested / opponent-reachable next)
    opp_adj = (adjacency @ opp.astype(np.int64)) > 0
    safe = E & ~opp_adj
    Af = adjacency.astype(np.float64)
    A = adjacency[moves]                       # (k, N)
    s1 = A & E[None, :]                        # (k, N) empty neighbours of each candidate
    # distance-2 shell: empty, neighbour of some s1, not c, not in s1
    reach2 = ((s1.astype(np.float64) @ Af) > 0) & E[None, :] & ~s1 & ~A
    # restrict to safe cells (not adjacent to opponent)
    safe2 = reach2 & safe[None, :]
    values = (safe2.astype(np.float64) @ pts) / 30.0
    return values

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Negative opponent follow-up swing: best (points grabbed + my points flipped back) over opponent claims after mine, minus my gain from the claim itself, /30, only counting opponent claims that would actually flip one of my cells."""
    N = owner.shape[0]
    my_home = int(homes[0])
    opp_home = int(homes[1])
    mine = (owner == 1)
    opp = (owner == -1)
    empty = (owner == 0)
    A1 = adjacency @ mine.astype(np.int64)
    Ao = adjacency @ opp.astype(np.int64)
    pts = points.astype(np.float64)
    idx_all = np.arange(N)
    not_my_home = idx_all != my_home
    not_opp_home = idx_all != opp_home
    Af = adjacency.astype(np.float64)

    out = np.zeros(moves.shape[0], dtype=np.float64)
    for idx in range(moves.shape[0]):
        c = moves[idx]
        adj_c = adjacency[c]
        flips = adj_c & opp & not_opp_home & ((A1 + 1) >= Ao)
        my_gain = pts[c] + pts[flips].sum()
        mine2 = mine.copy()
        mine2[c] = True
        mine2 |= flips
        opp2 = opp & ~flips
        A1b = adjacency @ mine2.astype(np.int64)
        Aob = adjacency @ opp2.astype(np.int64)
        legal_e = empty & (Aob > 0)
        if not legal_e.any():
            out[idx] = 0.0
            continue
        # cells of mine2 that opponent could flip back
        flip_back_mask = mine2 & not_my_home & ((Aob + 1) >= A1b)
        flip_back_pts = np.where(flip_back_mask, pts, 0.0)
        # opponent swing for claiming e: pts[e] + my flipped-back points adjacent to e
        gain = pts + Af @ flip_back_pts
        # only consider opponent claims that flip something of mine (aggressive grabs)
        flips_any = (Af @ flip_back_mask.astype(np.float64)) > 0
        aggressive = legal_e & flips_any
        if aggressive.any():
            best = gain[aggressive].max()
        else:
            best = 0.0
        out[idx] = -(best - my_gain) / 30.0
    return out
feature.measures: Negative opponent follow-up swing: best (points grabbed + my points flipped back) over opponent claims after mine, minus my gain from the claim itself, /30, only counting opponent claims that would actually flip one of my cells.

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """For each candidate: points of empty cells at distance 2 from it that the opponent cannot reach on its very next claim (no opponent-owned neighbour, not adjacent to c, not in the distance-1 shell), minus a penalty for distance-2 cells that ARE opponent-grabbable next turn — a signed safe/contested split, divided by 30."""
    E = (owner == 0)
    N = owner.shape[0]
    pts = points.astype(np.float64)
    opp = (owner == -1)
    # cells the opponent can claim next: empty with an opponent-owned neighbour
    opp_reach = E & ((adjacency @ opp.astype(np.int64)) > 0)
    mine = (owner == 1)
    my_reach = E & ((adjacency @ mine.astype(np.int64)) > 0)
    safe = E & ~opp_reach
    Af = adjacency.astype(np.float64)
    A = adjacency[moves]                       # (k, N)
    s1 = A & E[None, :]                        # empty neighbours of each candidate
    reach2 = ((s1.astype(np.float64) @ Af) > 0) & E[None, :] & ~s1 & ~A
    safe2 = reach2 & safe[None, :]
    # contested distance-2: cells that are opponent-reachable right now and that I can only reach in 2
    contested2 = reach2 & opp_reach[None, :] & ~my_reach[None, :]
    values = (safe2.astype(np.float64) @ pts - 0.5 * (contested2.astype(np.float64) @ pts)) / 30.0
    return values

feature.name: opponent_best_flip_against_candidate
feature.code:
import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Negative, per candidate, of the points at risk if the opponent claims its best-flipping empty neighbour next turn: for every empty cell adjacent to the candidate, simulate the opponent claiming it, sum the points of my cells it would flip, take the best (worst for me), /15. Zero if no such threat exists."""
    N = owner.shape[0]
    my = (owner == 1)
    opp = (owner == -1)
    empty = (owner == 0)
    my_home = homes[0]
    pts = points.astype(np.float64)

    A1 = adjacency @ my.astype(np.int64)
    Ao = adjacency @ opp.astype(np.int64)

    adj_c = adjacency[moves]                      # (k, N) neighbours of each candidate
    threat_cells = adj_c & empty[None, :]         # (k, N) empty cells opponent could grab next to c
    # restrict to cells the opponent can actually claim (adjacent to some opp cell)
    reachable = (Ao > 0)
    threat_cells = threat_cells & reachable[None, :]

    # For each (candidate, threat cell e): which of MY cells would flip if opp claims e.
    # opp claims e: Ao[j] + 1 >= A1[j]  for my cell j adjacent to e, j != my home.
    not_home = np.ones(N, dtype=bool)
    not_home[my_home] = False
    flip_cond_my = ((Ao[None, :] + 1) >= A1[None, :]) & my[None, :] & not_home[None, :]  # (1,N) which my cells would flip given e adjacent
    # flip_pts_vec[j] = points[j] if my[j] and flips
    flip_pts_vec = np.where(flip_cond_my[0], pts, 0.0)   # (N,)

    # For each candidate c and each threat cell e adjacent to c: value = sum over my neighbours of e of flip_pts_vec
    # = (adjacency @ flip_pts_vec)[e] summed over e in threat_cells[c]
    cell_flip_value = adjacency.astype(np.float64) @ flip_pts_vec   # (N,) points lost if opp claims each cell
    cell_flip_value = cell_flip_value * (~ (np.arange(N) == my_home))

    # best threat per candidate: max over e in threat_cells[c] of cell_flip_value[e]
    masked = np.where(threat_cells, cell_flip_value[None, :], -1.0)
    best = masked.max(axis=1)
    best = np.where(best < 0.0, 0.0, best)
    return -best / 15.0
feature.measures: Negative, per candidate, of the points at risk if the opponent claims its best-flipping empty neighbour next turn: for every empty cell adjacent to the candidate, simulate the opponent claiming it, sum the points of my cells it would flip, take the best (worst for me), /15. Zero if no such threat exists.

feature.code:
import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Negative of the points of the single highest-value empty cell that the opponent could claim next turn and that would flip one of my cells, divided by 5 — measures the worst immediate retaliation available to the opponent, only late in the game."""
    N = owner.shape[0]
    mine = (owner == 1)
    opp = (owner == -1)
    empty = (owner == 0)
    pts = points.astype(np.float64)
    my_home = homes[0]

    # My cells vulnerable to flipping: not my home, and opponent already has >= my count - 1 neighbours
    A1 = adjacency @ mine.astype(np.int64)
    Ao = adjacency @ opp.astype(np.int64)
    vulnerable = mine & (np.arange(N) != my_home) & (Ao + 1 >= A1)

    if not vulnerable.any():
        return np.zeros(moves.shape[0], dtype=np.float64)

    # For each empty cell e the opponent could claim (adjacent to opp territory),
    # which vulnerable cells would flip? A vulnerable cell j flips from e iff e is its neighbour
    # and after opp claims e: Ao[j]+1 >= A1[j] (already true by vulnerability).
    # Value of the retaliation = points of j (lost) captured via claiming e.
    # So value[e] = sum of points of vulnerable neighbours of e.
    vuln_pts = np.where(vulnerable, pts, 0.0)
    # opp-legal empties: empty cells adjacent to opponent territory
    opp_legal = empty & ((adjacency @ opp.astype(np.int64)) > 0)
    # retaliation value per empty cell
    retal = adjacency @ vuln_pts  # sum of vulnerable-neighbour points
    retal = np.where(opp_legal, retal, 0.0)

    # For each candidate: after my claim+flips, would reduce the opponent's opportunities.
    # Approximate: my claim removes one empty cell (the candidate) and flips some opp cells.
    # Score = -(worst retaliation remaining after my claim) / 5
    A1f = A1.astype(np.float64)
    Aof = Ao.astype(np.float64)
    not_home_mask = (np.arange(N) != homes[1])

    out = np.zeros(moves.shape[0], dtype=np.float64)
    for i, c in enumerate(moves):
        adj_c = adjacency[c]
        # flips from claiming c
        flips = adj_c & opp & not_home_mask & (A1f + 1.0 >= Aof)
        # after my claim: mine2, opp2
        mine2 = mine | flips
        mine2[c] = True
        opp2 = opp & ~flips
        # recompute vulnerability
        A1b = adjacency @ mine2.astype(np.int64)
        Aob = adjacency @ opp2.astype(np.int64)
        vuln2 = mine2 & (np.arange(N) != my_home) & (Aob + 1 >= A1b)
        vuln2_pts = np.where(vuln2, pts, 0.0)
        opp_legal2 = empty & ~np.eye(N, dtype=bool)[c] & ((adjacency @ opp2.astype(np.int64)) > 0)
        # opp_legal2: empty, not c, adjacent to opp2
        retal2 = adjacency @ vuln2_pts
        retal2 = np.where(opp_legal2, retal2, 0.0)
        worst = retal2.max() if retal2.size else 0.0
        out[i] = -worst / 5.0
    return out

feature.measures: Negative of the points of the single highest-value empty cell that the opponent could claim next turn and that would flip one of my cells, divided by 5 — measures the worst immediate retaliation available to the opponent, only late in the game.

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Sum of points of empty, opponent-unreachable cells at graph distance exactly 3 from each candidate, scaled by remaining-empty fraction and /30."""
    N = owner.shape[0]
    A = adjacency.astype(np.int32)
    D1 = A > 0
    D2 = (A @ A) > 0
    D3 = (D2.astype(np.int32) @ A) > 0
    M = D3 & ~D2 & ~D1  # shape (N, N): M[c, j] true iff dist(c, j) == 3

    opp = (owner == -1)
    opp_neighbour_count = A @ opp.astype(np.int32)  # per cell, number of opponent-owned neighbours
    safe = (owner == 0) & (opp_neighbour_count == 0)
    s = np.where(safe, points.astype(np.float64), 0.0)

    raw = M[moves].astype(np.float64) @ s  # shape (k,)
    value = raw / 30.0

    n_empty = int((owner == 0).sum())
    denom = max(N - 2, 1)
    decay = n_empty / denom
    return value * decay
